The CRA remains committed, of course, to upholding its procurement obligations in accordance with its policies and codes of conduct, as well as the Government of Canada's obligations.

The CRA's decision reflects a commitment to fairness, value and transparency in all procurement activities. The government, of course, remains committed to supporting Canadian workers, including veterans, and to upholding the principles of our trade agreements and procurement policies. It is imperative that Canadians have confidence in the CRA's processes and understand that decisions are made in their best interests, with a focus on delivering high-quality services while minimizing risks.

Madam Speaker, my question to the member, and he seems to be fairly informed, has two parts. First, the only reason CRA was able to issue this contract to a company other than Commissionaires was that Veterans Affairs removed the right of first refusal to Commissionaires, a policy that has been in place since 1945. The government refused to answer a question about that when I asked during question period. Maybe the member now knows why.

Second, I just want to clarify that, during his statement, the member said, I believe, that Allied Universal has maybe 12 Canadian veterans currently employed by the company. I point out that Commissionaires has over 4,000 Canadian veterans. Which one does he think would actually provide more employment opportunity, especially for older Canadian veterans?

Madam Speaker, just to correct the record, I said that, of the 60 security guards hired through that particular contract, 33 of them were former commissionaires while 12 of those served in uniform previously. Not all commissionaires served in uniform, apparently, from what I have been told. That is just to clarify for the member opposite what I said, to be factually correct.

As to the member's question about the procurement process, I think we would probably all agree that competition within procurement is a positive thing. A best value approach is probably the best way to evaluate procurement contracts. I will note that, within the buy Canadian policy, we have defined Canadian companies as not being determined by ownership criteria, but rather by the number of employment opportunities in Canada. This particular organization has 10,000 employees in Canada, so it did qualify under those criteria.

Members need to understand that the best value of this contract was weighed between a number of different factors, and this is the decision the CRA made. It stands by that decision. Even though I know it is hard for us and members opposite to accept that decision, it was the one determined to be in the best value, which is a balance of all the different criteria, as I mentioned, of quality, risk, employment and other factors within that procurement process.

Madam Speaker, on this, I find myself unequivocally agreeing with the member of Parliament for Bruce—Grey—Owen Sound and finding the argumentation from my friend, the parliamentary secretary, lacking because the fundamental piece around the best efficiencies, the best competitive bid, omits the commitment to buy Canadian.

The maple-washing point made by the leader of the official opposition would also apply to the $2 billion to General Dynamics for buying military equipment while claiming it is a Canadian company, although General Dynamics is a 100% U.S. company with a branch plant in London, Ontario. Canadians want to see investment in Canadian companies, first and foremost. So-called LNG Canada has not a single Canadian corporation involved. There are also PetroChina and Shell. I could go on.
Canadians really are calling for the government to put Canada first in procurement. I wonder if the parliamentary secretary could give us a sense of where that ranks when there are competing bids.

Madam Speaker, I appreciate the member opposite's question and comments. Just to be clear, the buy Canadian policy defines a company that qualifies as one not determined by who owns the company but rather by its significant operations within Canada, including employment opportunities. As I said, the contract in question here includes 10,000 employees in Canada. That is a significant base that supports the Canadian economy.

In terms of overall numbers, PSPC awarded a total of 1,644 new contracts for $23 billion. Some 1,342 of those contracts, worth roughly $17.7 billion, were awarded to Canadian suppliers. Again, the buy Canadian policy is real, and it is working. I know the members opposite keep pointing out instances, with some contracts, where perhaps there may be no Canadian supplier or a supplier does not have the same operations in Canada, and I think that it is weighing heavily upon the procurement decisions that are made by PSPC and the Treasury Board directives right across the government.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Sophie Chatel (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs and Associate Minister of National Defence, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Madam Speaker, with Remembrance Day now only nine days away, today we have a very important opportunity to remind Canadians that remembrance, commemoration and respect for the veterans in our communities have a place not only on November 11, but throughout the year, and for all Canadians. We owe that recognition to the women and men who have served and those who continue to serve our great country and protect our sovereignty.

It is in this spirit that I rise today to address the opposition motion. Respect for veterans and support for Canadian business deserve a serious debate. By treating a single contract as a measure of our government's respect for veterans, however, the opposition overlooks the breadth and the scale of the contribution they can make.

At committee, representatives of several veterans groups and organizations told us that we need to change the narrative about our veterans. We need to talk about their skills, training, experience and all they bring all of that to the civil workforce. Many leave the military at the age of 34. This is the average age of a veteran today, with years of working life ahead of them. What do they bring with them? They bring technical expertise in fields like airspace, cybersecurity and other dual-use technologies, including drones.

They are a tremendous asset in our country, particularly in those sectors where there is an acute labour shortage, yet the opposition motion focuses on their role in security services. Of course, our veterans are qualified for that work, but their opportunities extend way beyond that. They can help advance our industrial strategy, strengthen our defence industry and continue serving Canada in many different ways. That requires a lot more than a procurement decision. It requires the recognition of the skills and qualifications they acquired during their service. They need to put their expertise to work in industries that need them. That is precisely what our Minister of Veterans Affairs is working to deliver.
This motion gives me the opportunity to tell Canada's veterans about an important next step our government is taking to address today's realities and tomorrow's opportunities.

All across Canada, companies in many sectors are seeking qualified personnel to fill key strategic positions, expand their operations, and seize new business opportunities. Over the next 10 years, 593,000 new jobs in Red Seal trades will need to be filled. Trade schools will not be able to provide enough workers. In the aerospace sector alone, it is estimated that between 42,000 and 65,000 positions will need to be filled over the next 10 years. According to one study, trade schools will only be able to meet about 25% of that demand. At the same time, nearly 8,000 members of the Canadian Armed Forces leave military service each year, at an average age of 34.

Today, I would like to talk about how our government can bridge the gap between these two realities. In my view, veterans represent one of the largest untapped talent pools in the country. Their hands-on experience in logistics, operations, engineering, and information technology is a valuable asset for Canada as it seeks to diversify and expand its economic relationships around the world. When they want to embark on a new career, we must give them every opportunity to put that expertise to good use. We are doing this for veterans because they have served Canada and protected our sovereignty, but we are also doing it so that they can continue to contribute to Canada. We need them.

One point deserves to be highlighted. As I mentioned, today's veterans are, on average, quite young. They are seasoned professionals whose skills are in high demand, particularly in the dual-use technology sector, referring to technology that can be used both for military purposes and in our strategic industries. In addition to their technical expertise, Canada's veterans bring some even more highly valued assets to the table: strong leadership skills, problem-solving abilities, project management experience and a proven ability to perform under challenging and demanding conditions. Their expertise in logistics, cybersecurity, advanced technologies, human resources, finance and Red Seal trades deserves full recognition.

The challenge is that these fields are not the ones that immediately come to mind when we talk about military service. My colleagues are putting a lot of focus on security services. However, by limiting veterans to jobs in this field, we are missing an extraordinary opportunity to recognize their talent and expertise in leading trades. When a person did not serve in the military themselves and is unfamiliar with the military environment, it can be difficult for them to grasp the diverse range of skills that military personnel have. We are talking about acquired skills that are essential to modern military operations. More importantly, they are completely transferable to a civilian work environment. In many cases, they are exactly the skills that employers are looking for.

Canada, with our Minister of Veterans Affairs, is now taking deliberate steps to strengthen our defence industrial capacity, to invest in major projects and national development initiatives across the country, and to recognize the role that veterans can play in meeting that objective. We are living at a time when the demand for skilled workers will only continue to go grow. Last week, in Victoria, British Columbia, the Minister of Veterans Affairs announced a key initiative to encourage our veterans to contribute to our strategic defence industry following their military career. I am talking about the veteran employer recognition initiative and the new “Veteran Ready” designation, which recognizes organizations that value veterans' skills and that will commit to helping them transition to a successful civilian career in the field of their choice. This strategy sends a clear message to veterans, staff, clients and communities: This organization recognizes the value of military service, experience and leadership.

I therefore call on businesses and the general public across the country to show leadership in their local communities, raise awareness of this designation in their ridings, encourage businesses to take part in the initiative, help employers recognize the value of military experience, and help veterans find employment opportunities that match their skills.

Madam Speaker, first, I want to say that I agree with 95% of the member's speech. I fully endorse that our younger veterans, whose average age is 35, are capable of filling any job that Canadian industry and the Canadian job market have to offer. From social workers to public affairs officers to electrical technicians, they can do it all.

However, the question I asked the member last week was why Veterans Affairs removed the right of first refusal from the Commissionaires, a policy that has been in place since 1945. The older veteran commissionaires, on average, are in their late forties to early fifties. These are people who are just looking for work. They are already working for the Commissionaires, over 4,000 of them.

Why did the government remove the right of first refusal from the Commissionaires? They are not mutually exclusive. We can have both. We can be encouraging our veterans to work everywhere and helping to set up the right conditions, but at the same time, we should be supporting the Commissionaires, the largest non-profit employer of Canadian veterans.

Madam Speaker, security service are an important part of employment, and they will continue because our military personnel are good at them. They have the training, the experience, the knowledge and the security clearance to carry on in this job.

My point, and the focus of this government, is the much broader challenge that faces our veteran community. It is to find a rewarding career that really reflects the wealth of their experience and contributions and the fact that they are really technically savvy. They work with amazing dual-use technology. We need to have as a priority the recognition of their skills so they can have a rewarding career. They have many years to fulfill that.
Madam Speaker, I would like to congratulate the parliamentary secretary on her speech. I have the privilege of serving alongside her on the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs.

Let us be honest. Everyone in this House knows that the right of first refusal currently held by the Commissionaires organization—formerly known as the Canadian Corps of Commissionaires, which has existed since 1945 and just celebrated its 80th anniversary—will expire on March 31. Consequently, as of April 1, that right will no longer be on any government tender documents for security guard services anywhere in the government.

It seems to me that this runs counter to the discussions we have had at the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs, where we have been exploring ways to help veterans transition successfully into the labour market following their military careers.
My question is quite simple: Does the parliamentary secretary believe it makes sense to allow the right of first refusal to expire on March 31?
Madam Speaker, I thank my colleague for her question and for her work on the committee. I want to acknowledge the excellent work she does.

Security guard services are important, but I think this represents a very limiting view of the careers and experience of today's veterans. The average veteran is now just 34 or 35 years old. Our government's priority is not to find security guard positions for these veterans, because they possess extraordinary skills and can contribute to Canada's defence industrial strategy. When they transition to civilian life, they bring expertise in areas such as drones, cybersecurity and aerospace.

Moreover, this is not about the right of first refusal, because there are labour shortages in the aerospace sector, one of Quebec's flagship industries. Over the next 10 years, an average of between 42,000 and 65,000 positions will need to be filled, and there will be more than 8,000 new veterans each year who possess many of the technical skills required for those jobs.
The priority is skills recognition, and I encourage my colleagues to support it.
Madam Speaker, I would like to begin by saying that I will be sharing my time with the lovely member for Laurentides—Labelle.

What a pleasure it is for me to rise today as the Bloc Québécois critic for veterans affairs on this opposition day, when we are questioning certain government decisions regarding support provided to the Canadian Corps of Commissionaires.

First, let us remember that Remembrance Day is just a week away, and MPs from Quebec and Canada will be invited to participate in remembrance ceremonies by their local Royal Canadian Legion branches. In my riding, the ceremony hosted by the Valleyfield branch in Salaberry‑de‑Valleyfield will take place on Saturday, as will the ceremony in Beauharnois. The ceremonies in Huntingdon and Ormstown will take place on Friday. It is important for us, as MPs, to attend, but it is just as important to encourage our constituents to take part in these remembrance ceremonies. This is an opportunity to recognize the sacrifices of those who went to war, sometimes at the cost of their lives, their health or their family life. I encourage everyone to attend the ceremonies in their community and meet with veterans. I will be very pleased to attend, and I will take the time to listen to the veterans, because they have a lot to share with us.
The motion before us today is rather long and deals with several subjects, so I chose to focus my remarks on certain issues and on the Liberal government's choice to turn its back on veterans.

I was listening to my colleague, the parliamentary secretary, who argued that veterans are younger, that there is no question of sidelining them, that we need to modernize, that we have to accept this, that many jobs will be available, and that this justifies the right of refusal.

I want her to know that these things are not mutually exclusive. Currently, nearly 3,000 veterans work as security guards for the Commissionaires. They are worried right now. These veterans are used to holding a position that could disappear as of April 1. This could in fact be the case if the government's public tender and specifications do not specify that the Commissionaires have the first right of refusal. This refers to an arrangement where preference is given to companies that commit to hiring veterans for the positions.

This agreement has been in place for 80 years. The Canadian Corps of Commissionaires has been around since 1925. It was created specifically to support veterans, help them transition to civilian life and, above all, find employment. As we know, at the end of one's military career, continuing to be useful and contributing to the development of one's community is important for self-esteem and for what comes next. Now the Commissionaires are being deliberately abandoned. Frankly, I think I am choosing my words carefully, but I cannot put it any other way. The Commissionaires are being told that it is over. Now the government is awarding security contracts, at the lowest possible cost, to whichever company meets the criteria set out by Procurement Canada, and removing the right of refusal.

It is important to remember that this arrangement has been in place for 80 years, as I said, and has never really been a problem. I do not know why the government wants to get rid of it, because there is really no gain for veterans. Alternatively, if we keep it, there is really no loss for the government either.

The government keeps saying that veterans are important. A massive recruitment campaign is under way at the Department of National Defence to meet military targets. That means that a growing number of veterans will be reaching the end of their military careers and arriving at Veterans Affairs Canada. I fail to understand the logic of that, apart from saving on a few costs here and there. It is almost as if some public servant crunching numbers somewhere was told to modernize all that, because it mattered more.

Veterans, especially the Canadian Corps of Commissionaires, have taken that as a clear and unequivocal sign that veterans are no longer part of the current government's plans. A lot of people are no longer part of the current government's plans.

The environment might not be either, or Quebec SMEs. Now, it is our veterans' turn to be told that they are no longer part of the plans. As we know, however, the oil companies are part of the government's plans. There are data centres all over Alberta. They are part of the government's plans too, but continuing to support the Canadian Corps of Commissionaires is not.

I have a great deal of respect for the parliamentary secretary, but I hear her saying that this is not a particularly serious problem and that the government actually wants bigger things for veterans. It wants them to be more than security guards. It wants them to get more important jobs, value-added jobs.
I would simply reply that these things are not mutually exclusive.
When I hear the Minister of Finance and National Revenue talk about the loss of the Commissionaires' contract over a difference of $80,000, as stated in the motion, I am offended.

What offended me during this debate in the House was hearing people say that only about 60 employees will be impacted, about half of whom are veterans, and that those who wish to be rehired by the new company that was awarded the contract will have to accept a 14% pay cut. This is serious. The minister argued that this is an agency, that he cannot become involved in its decision-making and that he cannot intervene. He says it is an independent agency that made its own choices. It was the agency that decided not to include the Commissionaires' right of first refusal in its call for tenders.

The Liberal government had no qualms about ordering the CRTC to reconsider its decision to tax the digital giants. It intervened politically because the CRTC had reached a different conclusion than the one the government wanted. Now the Canada Revenue Agency has awarded a contract to a privately owned U.S. company, which does have Canadian subsidiaries, but which has made no commitment to keeping veterans on under the same employment conditions. That response is not only hard to understand; it is totally unacceptable.

If the government were truly committed to our veterans, it would have instructed the Canada Revenue Agency and all government agencies to include a requirement to hire a certain percentage of veterans in their calls for tenders. That is what we call political direction. No such direction was given. That is not surprising, given that the government has chosen to eliminate the right of first refusal altogether. This is a serious concern, and it is one of the issues we are highlighting today, seeing as most Quebeckers and Canadians are unaware of it.

Another thing that concerns me is that the government is just pumping out new agencies: agencies to handle cybersecurity, one to handle crime and money laundering, and yet another to deal with military procurement. What it all boils down to is that these agencies are all independent and the government is washing its hands of responsibility. When things go wrong, it will be the agencies' fault. There is no political accountability. That is what is worrisome today. We are seeing this with our veterans. The CRA's decision to drop the Commissionaires has led to a loss of jobs for our veterans.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Kevin Lamoureux (Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Madam Speaker, I will start off by indicating how much I personally value our veterans and the contributions they have made to our community. The government as a whole does too, and we see that in a number of policies that I could easily expand upon.

The question I have for the member is in regard to the CRA as an independent agency with an established criteria when something goes out to tender. Can she give her perspective as to the number of people in the Canadian Corps of Commissionaires who are veterans? Is the member aware of that? She gives the impression that they are all veterans. I am advising that that is not necessarily the case, even though they do outstanding work.

Madam Speaker, my colleague's question gives me an opportunity to clarify some things. I know that we are talking about the equivalent of 12 full-time positions for veterans. It is true that, when we talk about this, it seems that it is not a big number. However, that is not what is at issue. It is the principle that is at issue. Indeed, the CRA moved up the April 1 deadline by publishing specifications and exempting itself from the Commissionaires' right of refusal. That is what we are questioning here.

The fact that veterans representing 12 full-time equivalent positions are losing their jobs may seem insignificant to the parliamentary secretary. However, I think it is too many, because they already had a job. Moreover, those who stay will be paid $2 to $4 an hour less to do the same work.

Evidently, I cannot agree with the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance, who says that it is a small amount. No, it is not, because a right has just been taken away. Moreover, this is the first agency to decide to take this right away. Soon, on April 1, if the government does not change its mind, it would be the entire government, through Public Services and Procurement Canada, that will remove the Commissionaires' right of refusal.

Madam Speaker, I would like to thank my colleague for her hard work on the veterans affairs committee, which we both sit on. She was very flexible and was able to sub in as the chair recently due to an emergency and some challenging times.

The subject the committee is studying right now is veterans and employment. Does the member not find it absolutely ludicrous that at the time the committee is doing this study, which the Liberals brought forward, the Liberal government is going to be unemploying 3,000 veterans? Also, there was a witness who said out of frustration that this is not the first time we have studied this, and we are doing it again. What are her thoughts on that?

Madam Speaker, I want to thank my colleague. I enjoy serving with him on the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs. He is absolutely right. The Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs is looking for ways to improve veterans' employability and the transferability and recognition of their skills as they transition to the civilian workforce. The main issue is access to employment opportunities.

Right now, it seems as though the government is taking a step back. It is turning a blind eye and a deaf ear to veterans who are telling us that they need this historic partnership with the Commissionaires to continue.
We do not understand that inconsistency.

Madam Speaker, having served as vice-chair of the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs for a year, I cannot help but wonder: If veterans are so important, particularly when they return to civilian life, why ditch a decades-long tradition that supported our veterans?
Madam Speaker, it is hard to understand.
It costs nothing for the government to keep the program, yet it has a significant impact on veterans. As we speak, veterans are shocked and dismayed by the decision.
We hope that the government will change its mind and that, as of April 1, the Commissionaires will retain their right of first refusal.
Madam Speaker, some are attentive, while others are less so. My colleagues would do well to listen and learn from what I have to say today.

Last week in the House I spoke to Bill C-40, which seeks to create a Crown corporation for defence procurement. I was saying that creating the Crown corporation would be the end of transparency, accountability and the disclosure of choices and interests. I was also saying that I was concerned that the government would shirk responsibility for a decision that, in my opinion, was inconsistent and ill-advised.

As far as today's proceedings are concerned, I commend the Conservative Party's initiative on this issue, because this decision highlights exactly what I was talking about last week. Earlier, I mentioned that I had served as vice-chair of the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs, but I am also vice-chair of the Standing Committee on Government Operations and Estimates. My job as the Bloc Québécois critic for procurement is to shed light on government contracts.

The committee has a mandate to examine the technical aspects and the governance of choices and decisions. I met with some commissionaires this summer. I met with Marc Parent. I was shocked to learn that the government was planning on ending the long-standing tradition of hiring commissionaires for security services.

The Canadian Corps of Commissionaires has a long history, just recently celebrating their 100th anniversary. I was proud to be the critic for veterans affairs for a year, and I know the Minister of Veterans Affairs is passionate and dedicated to helping veterans transition into civilian life. A study on entrepreneurship is currently under way, and prior learning is being recognized. How can we help veterans make the transition easier?

Now veterans, the ones who are commissionaires, are being told that they do not matter, that they are not important enough to the government and that the government no longer believes in the core mission. They are being told that this contract is ending and that the government has decided instead to award it to an American company that has branches in Canada.
We need to be careful. How far does the buy Canadian policy go when it comes to doing business with Canadians?
The Liberals are telling us that this was an independent decision by the CRA and so no one is accountable. No one is responsible for this.

This just goes to show that the government wants to create corporations and agencies so that it can wash its hands of responsibility for decisions. That way, if people are unhappy, then it is not the government's responsibility. That is what is happening here.
This decision has serious consequences in terms of the message that it sends not only to our veterans but also to all legislators. That is a big part of our role.

I often talk about my role as a legislator because I do not think that people really understand it. Parliament is made up of elected officials from the government party and from the opposition parties. Our role, as the opposition, is to hold the government to account on behalf of the people we represent. We must ensure that the use of tax dollars and the government's decisions and policies are in keeping with the best interests of citizens. The government is taking away parliamentarians' ability to do their job for the sake of efficiency, but efficiency should not come at the cost of a loss of democratic oversight. That oversight is at the very heart of who we are.

It is the same thing with Canada Post. Canada Post is a Crown corporation. When we ask questions, the government tells us that the board of directors is responsible for decisions. That is an easy and convenient answer. However, Canada Post is in an untenable financial situation and has been for many years. We all know that.
Meanwhile, bonuses continued to flow freely even as the government was being called upon to cover the deficits.

The lack of transparency at Canada Post prevented parliamentarians, Quebeckers, Canadians and employees from obtaining a true, clear and accurate picture of the situation facing the Crown corporation.

It was under my leadership that the Standing Committee on Government Operations and Estimates launched a study of Canada Post. Despite our responsibility for overseeing public funds, we have been learning about changes at Canada Post through press releases and push notifications. That is not normal. It shows a blatant lack of respect for Parliament and for our democratic institutions.

The same can be said of the Crown corporation responsible for defence procurement. The government will tell us that decisions to purchase a particular aircraft, vessel or tank will be made by its board of directors. Billions of dollars will be invested in strengthening Canada's defence capabilities as the federal government seeks to meet NATO's target. Such procurement decisions must be subject to rigorous oversight. Let me be clear: taxpayers' money is not private money. When I spend money in my own businesses, I am free to do so and I bear the consequences. When it is my money, it is my business. That is not the case here. Public funds come from taxes and are entrusted to government through a social contract between citizens and the state to support the core functions of government.

When a government shirks certain democratic responsibilities in the name of efficiency, it is our duty to sound the alarm, ask questions and spark the necessary debates. The government is constantly running ads across all platforms, and that worries me greatly. Constituents regularly raise the issue when I am back in my riding. Slogans such as “build Canada strong” are everywhere. We are told that Canada must become its own best customer. The trouble is that it increasingly appears to be little more than a slogan, an ad campaign. Canadians are constantly being encouraged to believe they are the best, yet the government continues to award contracts to the lowest bidder.

In committee last week, the procurement ombud told members that it is imperative to ensure that government measures do not undermine Parliament's ability to do its job. He is concerned, and said so a number of times. Any such measures must respect the responsibilities entrusted to members of Parliament.

It will come as no surprise to anyone that the Prime Minister is running Canada like a business. A government is not a business. A government has obligations, including the obligation to be accountable to its citizens and carry out its moral duties. I am seriously concerned about these abuses. Our role as parliamentarians is to bring things to light and hold the government to account. Our role is also to ask hard questions and demand answers. That is why I am calling on members not to look away, but to pay attention to what is happening and to what the government is doing.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Kevin Lamoureux (Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Madam Speaker, I have said a great deal about our veterans and how much we value them and will continue to work to support them.

My question for the member is in regard to subsidiary companies in general, and it is more on the principle of them. Does the member recognize that there is a lot of crossover between the United States and Canada on subsidiaries and that it works both ways? There are subsidiaries owned by American companies that have a large footprint here in Canada, and vice versa. Does the member believe in principle that companies with subsidiaries that are located in Canada and have a substantial footprint should be incorporated into any form of buy Canada policy?
Madam Speaker, I thank my colleague for his question, because I did not have time to say everything.

The procurement ombud told us last week that enough data is available to evaluate the buy Canadian policy and determine where things stand. We need to look at the criteria to determine what is working well and what would be worthy of the buy Canadian stamp.

For the time being, however, the focus is on maximizing participation and access for Canadian businesses, which need opportunities to work in light of the current geopolitical environment. We will get the documents from the procurement ombud, and the Standing Committee on Government Operations and Estimates will study them before coming back to the House on this issue.
Madam Speaker, I would like to thank my colleague, someone I spent some time with at the veterans affairs committee. She is surely missed, but she has been well replaced.

My colleague from across the aisle asked a question about principle. It was a very good question to ask. The principle of this is why we brought this motion forward as an opposition day motion. It is the principle of putting veterans first, those who have sacrificed their lives for the freedoms we have and for us to be able to speak freely in this House.
I would like to hear my colleague's thoughts on the principle of this opposition motion.

Madam Speaker, the point is not only to speak out, but also to correct course. If we truly want to support veterans, the Prime Minister must start by listening to his minister, who is trying to do the right thing, and take action. Right now, veterans are being left behind, and that saddens me greatly.

Madam Speaker, I hope that the member for Winnipeg North is listening to my question, because I am going to give him the figures he asked me for earlier. I have them in front of me. The Canada Revenue Agency chose not to maintain the Commissionaires' right of first refusal. What has been the result? The government keeps talking about 12 veterans, but that figure actually represents a volume of work equivalent to 12 full-time positions. In reality, the decision affects about 50 veterans. Most of those who were selected chose either to retire or to transfer to other Commissionaires contracts rather than accept the pay cut imposed by the new private-sector provider. Does the member believe that is acceptable?

Madam Speaker, people are focusing on critical mass, but I think we need to step back and look at the quality of the program and what we are actually trying to achieve. Yes, there is a number involved. To take the example of Cúram, one could argue that only 33,000 seniors were affected among millions, but that is not the point. The point is that we had a legitimate model that supported veterans in their transition to civilian life. What is happening now is unacceptable, which is why I welcome the Conservatives' opposition day motion.

Madam Speaker, it is a pleasure to rise today to speak to this important motion. I note that I will be splitting my time with my hon. colleague, the member for Moose Jaw—Lake Centre—Lanigan, who is a veteran. Like other veterans in the House, I want to thank him for his service.

I want to take this opportunity to remind and encourage Canadians to wear a poppy. It is a very small but really important gesture that we can take as we lead up to Remembrance Day. October 24 is now designated as the date we are going to start wearing our poppies every year. The Royal Canadian Legion has set it, so it should be easier for us to remember than the time change.

It is so important that we engage in the act of remembrance. In fact, it is an obligation we have, one that I know all members of the House take very seriously. When we find areas of common agreement, we should really lean into those and take them as an instruction on how we should carry things all the way forward.

That leads to the subject of the motion we are considering today. It has two broader contexts that I want to address. I have spoken to the importance of remembrance, the duty we have to the men and women who have done their duty for us, for Canadians. They have afforded us the privilege of living in a democracy and a free and fair country, and in a place where when we have elections, power is changed without a shot being fired. This is done on the backs of the men and women who have put on the uniform to defend our basic freedoms. This is the first thing.

Once they are done with their service to us and once they have taken the uniform off for the last time, what do we owe to them? I would say the dignity that comes from employment is one area where we can fulfill our obligation to our veterans. Another is that we deliver on making sure we help them get well from any injuries or illnesses that arise from their service. This is not something we do a great job of in this country. It is something we need to do better on, and I am committed to that work, along with my colleagues. Employment is something we can work on. As legislators, it is something we can do in this place. How can we create opportunities for veteran employment?

The second thing I want to talk about is the current time we are in. We are in the midst of a trade war with our neighbours to the south, and it has come as a result of President Trump, frankly, starting a trade war with us while we had a trade deal with the U.S. In the face of that, the Liberal government has said that we need to buy Canadian. I agree. I agree that we need to prioritize buying Canadian now more than ever. We should be making sure that Canadian firms are fulfilling federal contracts.

Should we do both things at the same time? Should we be making sure that we create employment opportunities for our veterans at the same time that we are buying Canadian? I would say yes. I think that is a pretty natural fit.

We have the case of the security contract of $12 million for the CRA. The contract was awarded to a subsidiary of an American company that is affiliated with and linked to Trump, to the U.S. president. The company is carrying out work for the Trump administration and for ICE. ICE is in the headlines for all the wrong reasons. We do not necessarily need to get deeply into that issue. We generally get it, and I do not think we want it. I do not think we want to import that here.

The CRA had the opportunity to award this contract to the firm in question, the Trump-linked company, or to a Canadian not-for-profit, the Canadian Corps of Commissionaires. It is the largest non-governmental employer of veterans in Canada. It employs more than 4,000 veterans. How do I know that it is the largest employer of veterans? I checked and the Canadian War Museum provides that figure for us.

The difference in the bids for these two companies, the American firm and the Canadian not-for-profit firm, was less than 1%. I am talking about $80,000. What are our obligations here? Are we buying Canadian? Are we creating employment opportunities for veterans? When we first pointed this out to the government, I expected its response would have been muted, but it would have done the right thing. I was frankly quite surprised that it doubled down on it.

What we want to do with this motion is give the government the opportunity to get it right. I think the timing is really important. We want to signal to veterans and to their families that we are going to prioritize employment opportunities for Canadian veterans. We need to look at the timing of this in the face of this ongoing trade dispute with the U.S. We should be sending a message to Canadian businesses that we are going to prioritize government contracts to Canadian firms.

The government has the opportunity to do what I would say is the right thing. I think we would agree that it is the right thing to do. That is what we are asking for today. We are asking for the government to reverse the decision to award this contract to a firm that has questionable ties and instead award it to a Canadian company.

Does that need to be the Commissionaires? I have spoken to its bona fides as an employer of Canadian veterans, but I think the first principle we should be applying here is buying Canadian, and then we need to be giving consideration to the employment opportunities that we are creating for veterans. Let us commit ourselves to that. Let us recommit ourselves to the opportunities that we are creating for Canadian veterans.

I am not asking what is the most we can do, but as a country and as legislators, when we are setting the direction and the priorities for the federal government, I do think that this is probably the least we can do. The least we can do is buy Canadian in the face of this trade dispute. I think that creating these employment opportunities for veterans is the least we can do for the men and women who have served our country with unlimited liability.

With that, I want to take one more opportunity to encourage Canadians to engage in an act of remembrance, to attend a cenotaph service in their community or to thank a veteran. They do not need to want to be thanked for someone to thank them. I encourage Canadians to wear a poppy, and to keep in their thoughts the families and the brothers and sisters in arms of those who were killed and injured in the tragic events in Wainwright of late. If someone is a person of faith, I encourage them to say a prayer for them.
I encourage Canadians to reflect on the fact that we do live in the greatest country in the world, and we owe so much of that to the men and women of the Canadian Armed Forces and our veterans.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Caroline Desrochers (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Housing and Infrastructure, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Madam Speaker, I want to thank the member for his service.

I am just wondering if the member is aware that, under our government, we have done so much in support of veterans, including over these last few months, such as the disability benefit, which we have invested in for over four years. Just last week, we launched a veteran employer recognition initiative, which is going to help veterans with finding a job. We are making health care more accessible.
The parliamentary secretary has done a great deal of work on this file during her tenure.
How does the hon. member feel about the fact that when the Conservatives were in power, they closed nine Veterans Affairs offices across the country? We reopened them under this government.
I would like to know how he feels as a former member of the Armed Forces.

Madam Speaker, as a legislator today, who has committed himself to serving veterans and to serving all Canadians, I can tell members that what I am hearing from veterans is that they are not interested in focusing exclusively on the rearview mirror. If we want to compare outrages on where the government has fallen down over the last 11 years, I think it is a damning indictment of the government and our service to veterans. If we want to compare the government before that, I think it is a damning indictment of how this place has served our veterans, and the government before that as well. I think that we can commit ourselves today to doing better for veterans. That is what I am asking for.

Is there some good news for veterans that the government has announced? Sure, there is. Is there more to do? Do we need to get wait times down? Do we need the government to meet even just its own service delivery standards, which are far too long? Absolutely, we do. Let us commit collectively to doing better today.
Madam Speaker, I congratulate my Conservative colleague on his speech.

I find today's motion particularly compelling for a number of reasons. First, the national poppy campaign is in full swing. Nearly every member of the House is proudly wearing a poppy in remembrance of those who fought, and those who gave their lives, for our freedom and our values.

Against that backdrop, we are confronted with a situation that, in my view, is nothing short of an insult to our veterans, whom we have pledged to honour and whom we are sincerely honouring, I would hope, during this special week.

Can my colleague tell us a bit more about the fact that, during the last election campaign, the parties generally agreed to implement a buy Canadian, buy local policy and to implement measures that promote buying from local companies and groups?

What message does it send to veterans that they were passed over in favour of an American company with ties to ICE and a questionable track record? I would like to hear my colleague's comments about the sensitivity that should have been shown to this group of individuals whom we are honouring during this special week.

Madam Speaker, we can see quite plainly that this decision does not align with what are plainly Canadian values. It is not aligned with what Canadians expressed in the last election. Most importantly, I think the motion and the discussion today measure the Prime Minister's words against his actions. We want him to make good on what Canadians expect him to do. They expect him to do it because he said he was going to. We want the government to buy Canadian. We want it to honour our veterans.

I think that this choice, frankly, is diametrically opposed to what Canadians want. It is antithetical to what the government says it believes and what it will do. We want to create opportunity for Canadian firms, but we also need to send a message. What are Canadian values? What do we believe? Who are we going to stand up for? If we are not standing up for Canadian businesses and if we are not standing up for the men and women of the Canadian Armed Forces, what are we doing here?

There is an opportunity for the government to do the right thing. The Liberals can reverse the decision and award this contract to a Canadian firm because it is the right thing to do and it is what they said they were going to do.

Madam Speaker, from my perspective, to start off, I would like to acknowledge the generational remembrance that we have. Not too many people can see this, but in the gallery we have some young girls who are wearing poppies right now and they are sitting with their family of many generations. That is heartwarming. I will not name them because I do not know them, but I just want to thank them for wearing a poppy and for supporting our troops, and that is what we are here to talk about.

I am proud to rise in support of this motion. In a few days, we will gather at cenotaphs in every town in this country. In Moose Jaw, in Lanigan, in Watrous and in Outlook, people will stand in the cold to keep two minutes of silence. Remembrance is about a promise. We promise those who serve that we will not forget them and that we will keep faith with them.

In 1945, Canada made a simple commitment. When Ottawa needed its buildings guarded, it would call the Canadian Corps of Commissionaires first, because the corps hired the people who came home. That policy was created under Mackenzie King and kept by 12 prime ministers after him, Liberals and Conservatives alike. A Conservative government reaffirmed the policy in 2006 and widened it to include RCMP members. It took this Prime Minister to end it. This year, the Liberals ended the policy with a letter, but with no real explanation, no meaningful consultation and no replacement.

We are talking about roughly $350 million a year and about 8,000 guards at federal sites. More than 3,000 of them are veterans. The government's own briefing notes said it was engaging with stakeholders. The Commissionaires say they were never consulted. They have had to go to Federal Court just to be heard. The government says veterans are not working enough of the hours, but the government sets the wages on those contracts and the Commissionaires say that they have drifted toward minimum wage. The government sets the wages, then blames the court. If the target is broken, they should fix the target. The Commissionaires' court filing says a former deputy minister proposed exactly that. Instead, the government scrapped the program and kept the excuse.

This year, the government is breaking that promise. It is ending an 80-year commitment to give veterans a job when they come home, and it is handing their work to a lower bidder, even when its buy Canadian policy says otherwise.

Then came the Canada Revenue Agency contract. When the Trump administration launched its trade war, the Prime Minister promised that whenever Ottawa spends, it would select Canadian suppliers by default. In April, he promised to build Canada strong with Canadian steel, Canadian aluminum, Canadian lumber and Canadian workers. Then in June, with the CRA security contract, nearly $12 million went to the Canadian subsidiary of an American multinational over a Canadian not-for-profit that is the country's largest employer of veterans. The difference between bids was $80,000, less than 1%.

To put that in perspective, according to the government's own answer to an Order Paper question, the Prime Minister's delegation spent $175,000 on in-flight catering during one 10-day trip to China, Qatar and Davos this January. The gap in the cost to veterans is less than half of that.
An hon. member: Oh, oh!
Fraser Tolmie: I know where you're going with that. I will deal with it later.
The Assistant Deputy Speaker (Alexandra Mendès): I am not going anywhere.

Fraser Tolmie: Madam Speaker, this is not about one company. The question is what the government asked for, and keeping veterans on was not part of it. The government says that 12 veterans kept their jobs under this contract. Twelve is a number they found after the fact. Nothing in that contract required a single veteran to be hired. Canadian steel, Canadian aluminum, Canadian lumber, Canadian workers; apparently not Canadian veterans. A slogan is not a policy.

Every time we have asked about this contract, the government has given the same answer. The Secretary of State told the House, “Politicians are not involved in these decisions.” It is hands off. However, this fall, the House has been debating Bill C-40, the government's new defence procurement agency. Under that bill, the minister would be able to direct the agency's procurement, and it would have to comply, as an associate minister would get direction over a $1-billion fund that can lend money and buy shares. The bill would give the government 17 ways to skip open competition.

When it is $1-billion defence contracts, the government wants both hands on the wheel. When it is veterans' jobs and its own buy Canadian policy, suddenly it is hands off. That tells us where its priorities are.

Bill C-40 would rewrite how Canada buys for its military, and it does not contain a single target for veteran-owned businesses nor one credit for companies that hire veterans. The United States sets goals for veteran-owned businesses in federal funding contracting. The Canadian government already knows how to set procurement targets when it wants to. Veterans do not get one. In one year, the government ended the right of first refusal, let veterans lose the CRA contract over $80,000 and wrote a defence procurement with no place for veterans. That is not an accident. It is a pattern.

I have sat on the veterans affairs committee since 2021. In that time, we have come back to debate veterans' work transition over and again. Every one of those studies lands in the same place: Meaningful work after service is one of the biggest factors in veterans' well-being. Therefore, what I cannot square is that at this very moment, our committee is studying how to get veterans into good jobs, but the government is ending the one federal procurement policy built to do exactly that, and there is no plan to replace it. Nothing says how many veterans would be hired, or where, or how anyone would know.

When I was the mayor of Moose Jaw, we had a rule: If we cannot measure it, we cannot manage it. The government is scrapping the one veterans jobs program it could actually measure and is replacing it with nothing.

Conservatives believe that a promise to a veteran is a promise we keep. The motion before us asks the government to do three simple things: First, respect veterans; second, follow its own buy Canadian policy; and third, have the Prime Minister reverse the CRA security contract.

None of this is complicated. It is a question of whether the government means what it says. In a few days, at the cenotaph in Moose Jaw, the last post will sound, and we will fall silent. We will remember the people who kept the promise they made to this country. The least we can do is keep ours to them: a job when they come home and a government that means what it says.

We want to thank the veterans of Moose Jaw—Lake Centre—Lanigan who are serving at 15 Wing and at Dundurn, those across our country and those who serve alongside them, as well as their families. Veterans kept their promise to Canada. Conservatives will make sure Canada keeps its promise to them.

I would like to recognize a lot of people within our community and in Parliament who are veterans. I would like to thank my colleague who is the critic for Veterans Affairs for his service, and a few other fellow members. This means a lot to us. That is why we brought the motion forward. It means a lot to Canadians. We are pleading with the Prime Minister to make the decision to change his mind on this and recognize that it is okay to humble himself and say that he was wrong.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Kevin Lamoureux (Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Madam Speaker, I do not believe it was intentional, but I wonder if the member recognizes that he somewhat misled the House earlier when he implied that 3,000 veterans would be affected or fired. Could he provide clarification on the actual number of veterans, if he actually knows?

Madam Speaker, I would like to thank my colleague from across the aisle. I know he served in the military, and I respect his time in service. It is obviously something he is very passionate about and understands.

The fact that the government is cancelling this contract to support a company that is supporting Trump's ICE detention program is distasteful. Canadians want better and expect better from their government.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Bob Zimmer (Prince George—Peace River—Northern Rockies, CPC):

Content.ParaText: Madam Speaker, I think most Canadians have heard the debate today and they go back to the Prime Minister's having made promises about buying Canadian and supporting Canadians. That is why most of us find it very strange that the CRA did not give a security contract to a top patriotic organization, arguably the most patriotic organization, in Canada, the Commissionaires, but to what Newsweek called a top patriotic company in the U.S.
I will ask the member whether he thinks it is appropriate to give the contract to the most patriotic Canadian company, or to the most patriotic American company.
Madam Speaker, obviously I am pro-Canadian. We should be supporting our troops and our veterans. When they come home, they want meaningful employment.

One of the things not being touched on here is that veterans who come home, when they leave the military, go through a bit of an identity crisis. Giving them meaningful employment is something that helps with their mental well-being. Therefore, it is a complete slap in the face to Canadian veterans when they come home and find fewer opportunities for employment in the workforce in Canada.
Madam Speaker, I want to begin by commending my colleague on his speech.
On the issue of respect for our veterans and our armed forces, we are on the same page. I think it is important to acknowledge that today.

On the issue of buying local, I cannot get over it. The government's decision not to make good on the commitments made by the Prime Minister himself is quite troubling. I do not understand it. I still cannot make sense of it.

That said, I have a serious question that is kind of underlying all of this. In his opinion, have any studies been conducted on safety issues? Has any study been conducted to determine whether or not it is safe to transfer such significant responsibilities, which affect all Canadians and Quebeckers, to a private agency under U.S. jurisdiction? I must admit that I am quite concerned about this.
Madam Speaker, that is a good question.

I am not aware of any study, but that is a big concern and a big red flag. I ultimately trust veterans who have put their life on the line for our country, including for the province of Quebec. I have served with many Quebeckers who are very proud. This is a big concern and a big red flag I would have. What happens in a few years if we find that something has gone wrong and the agency has not been properly vetted?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Kevin Lamoureux (Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Madam Speaker, it is always a pleasure to rise and to address the issue of our Canadian Forces, and indeed of our veterans.

As did a number of members of the House, I had the honour of serving in the Canadian Forces. I served for just over three years. One of the things I reflect on in a very positive way is when this time of the year came around and our regiment, members of the Canadian Forces posted in Lancaster Park, participated in parades. Among the people I had the honour of marching alongside were the World War II veterans in particular. We understood the value of and gained an appreciation for the sacrifices they had made. After the parade, we would go to other destinations, and they would talk about some of the things that had taken place during World War II.

I have the deepest respect for the people who served and who gave the ultimate sacrifice of their life, and for those who have served in the Canadian Forces in whatever capacity, as well as for their supporters, whether it is DND or the families and so forth.

I know I am not alone. Whether it is the Prime Minister, any member of the Liberal caucus or, I would suggest, all members of the House of Commons, we recognize the contributions of our veterans in the past, in the present and going into the future.

We have seen that, to a certain degree, government actions over the last 18 months are setting a positive trend towards our Canadian Forces. We would have to look back generations to find the last time when there were as many Canadians wanting to join the Canadian Forces. When it comes to our veterans, we have put policies in place. A specific example is that in 2025, we put a significant amount of money in the budget so we could advance IT services so veterans would be able to receive their disability benefits more quickly.

We do not need a lesson from the Conservatives on veterans and services. I would remind my Conservative friends across the way that there was a day when I was in opposition, and those were the days when Conservative policy was made that led to the shutting down of nine Veterans Affairs offices in the country. Fortunately, with the change in government, those offices were reopened. That was something that meant a great deal to me personally and to a vast majority of members of the House of Commons in 2015.

We can think about the Canadian Corps of Commissionaires. I understand that the history, in good part, of that organization is as a non-profit. We need to recognize that when it was brought in during the late 1920s or the 1930s, around the time of World War I, it was because of those veterans. If we go to the 1920s, before it was really identified as a national organization, it started off in Montreal. By the time we got into the mid- or late-1930s, that is when it became well established as a national organization, and it was because of our veterans. Let us look at World War II and the number of veterans who were engaged, involved and employed. Governments back then saw the merit of the Canadian Corps of Commissionaires.

However, let us do the comparison. I will say that I am a very strong fan of the Commissionaires. I have met with Commissionaires in the past, both at the Manitoba legislature and in my MP constituency office, and I can say that the work they do is incredible.
Today, we will find that about 20% of them are veterans, but do not quote me on that. Contrast that with the day the Commissionaires came into being. When it came into being—
I am sorry to interrupt the member. The debate will continue after question period, and the hon. member will have 14 minutes and 41 seconds.

Mr. Speaker, today, I rise to recognize the 50th anniversary of Haahuupayak Elementary School, located on the traditional territory of Tseshaht First Nation. Since 1976, Haahuupayak has been far more than a school. Its name comes from the Nuu-chah-nulth word meaning “teaching with love”. It has been a place where generations of children have grown up surrounded by indigenous culture, language and community and a strong sense of identity and belonging. For five decades, this remarkable school has helped preserve and strengthen cultural knowledge while empowering young people through education.

I want to thank the elders, knowledge-keepers, educators, staff, families and community members whose dedication has made this possible. I am incredibly proud to support Haahuupayak and its important work.
On behalf of the people of Courtenay—Alberni, congratulations on 50 extraordinary years of education, culture and language. Klecko klecko.

SubjectOfBusiness.SubjectOfBusinessTitle: Municipal and Provincial Elections in British Columbia

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, it has been a very busy few weeks in B.C. with both municipal and provincial elections. I want to take a moment to congratulate all newly elected and returning MLAs and mayors, as well as all city councillors and school board trustees elected across New Westminster—Burnaby—Maillardville.

First, in New Westminster, I congratulate mayor-elect Daniel Fontaine, who will be sworn in today, as well as returning MLA Jennifer Whiteside. I also want to recognize Mayor Patrick Johnstone for his 16 years of service to the city of New Westminster.
In Burnaby, I congratulate Mayor Mike Hurley and returning MLA Raj Chouhan.
In Coquitlam, I congratulate newly elected mayor Craig Hodge and MLA Matt Liang. I want to thank MLA Jennifer Blatherwick for her service to Maillardville.
Lastly, I want to congratulate Premier-elect Lorne Doerkson on his decisive victory.

These elections bring new ideas and perspectives to our communities. I look forward to working together with all on shared priorities like affordability, infrastructure, education, health care and public safety. Congratulations.
Mr. Speaker, November, also known as “Bowvember”, is a perfect time to talk about men's mental and physical health, especially prostate health.

I want to acknowledge QUB columnist Richard Martineau, who had the courage to speak openly about his prostate cancer. I was moved by his frank, uncensored and very detailed account, and it convinced me to share my own experience as a cancer survivor in great detail, I must say.

I am familiar with the worries, questions and emotions that come with such a diagnosis. I know I am not alone. Constant, Marc, Mario and hundreds of others have been through this. More and more men are surviving thanks to science, but my thoughts go out especially to the families of those who sadly lost their fight.

As I proudly wear this bow tie today, and I will be wearing the Procure one when I receive it, I want to send a simple message to all men. They should take care of themselves and not hesitate to consult experts, share their concerns and ask for help. This is also true when it comes to mental health and suicide prevention.
Let us be brave and have the courage to speak with our doctor or a loved one about it. It is easier when we are not alone.
I want to thank Richard Martineau.
Mr. Speaker, today, I rise to mark the 40th anniversary of the Heyez chocolate factory, a wonderful company located in Mont-Saint-Bruno—L'Acadie.
This business has been bringing joy to people in our region since 1986. It is part of our lives, our celebrations and our special moments with family.

Behind this wonderful story are passionate people and a hard-working team. I especially want to commend Karolanne Pomerleau and Jérôme Savoie‑Lemay for their hard work and dedication. The Heyez chocolate factory is a true pillar of Mont-Saint-Bruno—L'Acadie. It is helping to build a vibrant community, create jobs and attract people to our region. It is also a fine example of how local businesses play a vital role in our communities.
I want to congratulate them on 40 years in the chocolate business and wish them continued success.

Mr. Speaker, as Remembrance Day approaches, we pause to honour those who never came home while also remembering those who did. Some returned carrying wounds we can see. Others carry wounds we cannot. More than 2,000 Canadians were wounded during the Afghanistan mission. This year, 39 more were injured in the tragic fire at CFB Wainwright.

Behind every injury is a life forever changed, a family forced to adapt and a burden carried long after the headlines fade. A damaged limb, a lingering burn, chronic pain or the invisible weight of post-traumatic stress can alter a life forever, yet our veterans and serving members continue to show remarkable courage through recovery, rehabilitation and daily struggle.
As we gather in remembrance, let us honour not only the fallen, but also the wounded. Their sacrifice did not end when the battle was over. It lives on, quietly and courageously, every single day.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to mark the 18th anniversary of Valora and commend its founder, Maria Larosa Napolitano, for her commitment to women who are the victims of domestic violence. For 18 years, Valora has been rallying the community and raising funds to support women's shelters in the Lanaudière, Laurentian and Laval regions. These shelters give survivors a safe space and the support they need to rebuild their lives. Valora's next event will take place on November 8 in Rosemère.
Every woman deserves to live free from violence, with dignity and hope. Supporting survivors is a collective responsibility that requires lasting community commitment.
I want to congratulate Maria Larosa Napolitano, the volunteers and all those who contribute to this essential mission.

Mr. Speaker, in 1925, the Commissionaires were founded on one commitment: that those who served Canada would come home and not be forgotten. Today, it is the largest private sector employer of veterans in Canada, standing watch at federal buildings across the country.

This year, that commitment was betrayed. With the single stroke of a pen, the Minister of Veterans Affairs ended the right of first refusal instead of working with the Commissionaires to modernize the agreement. Despite that order not taking effect until next year, the CRA awarded a security contract to the subsidiary of an American company that holds contracts with ICE and the Trump deportation program.

At election time, the Liberals wrap themselves in our flag, and at contract time, they pay Americans. The Prime Minister promised that Canada would be its own best customer. Veterans were promised that they would not be forgotten. Both promises are broken. I call on the government to restore the right of first refusal, to work with the Commissionaires and to support our opposition day motion.
Mr. Speaker, housing with health care supports attached means more health, more dignified living and safer communities for all. In south Parkdale, it is happening.

Dunn House, a project of the University Health Network, in partnership with Fred Victor, United Way Greater Toronto, West Neighbourhood House, 51 residents and their neighbours on Dunn Avenue and across south Parkdale, is delivering health care. Emergency room visits are down 52%, and hospital stays are down 79%. Behind these numbers are people like Jason Miles, whose powerful story and continued advocacy remind us that a safe home offers more than shelter. It offers dignity, stability and the opportunity to rebuild a life.

I want to thank Dr. Kevin Smith, Dr. Andrew Boozary, LP Pavey and all the people at UHN and beyond whose advocacy and leadership have helped turn this vision into a reality. I also thank Build Canada Homes and the Minister of Housing and Infrastructure.

What began with 51 homes in Parkdale is now growing into a model for hundreds more, including 83 units in south Parkdale. Supportive housing does not just save public dollars. It saves lives and brings dignity. I look forward to seeing this model, which began in Parkdale, continue to expand across the country.

Mr. Speaker, in Niagara, trade with the U.S. is not just a talking point. It is a paycheque and a lifeline for tens of thousands of workers. My riding is home to the Peace Bridge, the third-largest commercial border crossing in Canada. The Welland Canal bisects my riding and is literally the beating heart of the St. Lawrence Seaway. Every truck, every ship and every job depends on a working relationship with the United States.
Canadians are tired, and they need a trade deal now. Time is not our friend, but all we hear is talk and no action.

This weekend, the Prime Minister called six by-elections and then called Donald Trump. It is time the Prime Minister did what he said he would do. Canadians did not elect a performer. They were promised a negotiator. We need a good deal for Canadians. He needs to get the deal done, and he needs to get it done now.

Mr. Speaker, this year we are celebrating the 100th birthday of Suzanne Guité. This great, internationally renowned artist from the Gaspé was born in New Richmond and based in Percé. Suzanne Guité was a sculptor, painter and muralist who trained under international masters. In 1956, she founded the Centre d'art de Percé. She made a name for herself in North America and Europe, from Expo 67 to the Venice Biennale.

Admitted to the Royal Canadian Academy of Arts in 1975, she was recognized this summer as a historical figure of Quebec. From the mural La Justice est l'Espoir de l'Homme at the New Carlisle Courthouse to her work Terre des hommes along the Rideau Canal here in Ottawa, Ms. Guité's presence still fills our spaces.
Let us pay tribute to her and remember a woman who left us far too soon under horrific circumstances. I join the people of the Gaspé in calling for a postage stamp to be issued in her honour.

Mr. Speaker, the world is changing, and so are the threats facing our country. Last week, our government launched the plan for a stronger Canada, our first national security strategy in more than 20 years. It starts with a simple truth. Today, economic security is national security. That is why our plan is focused on securing our supply chains and strategic industries; rebuilding our Canadian Armed Forces; protecting Canadians from foreign interference, espionage and organized crime; and modernizing our intelligence capabilities.

In London West, we know what this means. Our workers, our manufacturers and our innovators help power Canada's economy, and they are part of how we keep this country strong and keep this country moving forward.

National security is not just about protecting our borders. It is about protecting our people, our jobs, our livelihoods and the future that we want to build together. That is why this plan is really important at this particular moment, and this plan is going to deliver exactly what Canadians are needing in this moment.

Mr. Speaker, homebuilding is down, food bank lineups are up, growth has flatlined, and the Prime Minister has broken his own fiscal anchors, piling on more debt that our children will pay for. That is the record, so he plays a trump card.

Last week, he told Politico he could wait two and a half more years without a trade deal. Then, moments after calling the by-elections, he changed his tune. He called the by-elections and then he called Trump. What a coincidence. We have seen this by-election movie before. Canadians do not need more theatre. They do not need another month-long circus designed to distract from Liberal failures here at home. They need results.

The Prime Minister promised Canadians a great deal. He campaigned on it, so he should deliver it. We need tariff-free trade with our biggest customer so our workers can get to work, not more photo ops, not more grandstanding and certainly not more cynical phone calls timed to by-election campaigns.

SubjectOfBusiness.SubjectOfBusinessTitle: National Skilled Trades and Technology Week

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, today we kick off National Skilled Trades and Technology Week. The aim is to raise awareness about skilled trades and technology careers among youth, parents, educators and the public.

Our government is committed to building a stronger economy, and a large part of that includes young people choosing skilled trades and careers in technology. In my riding of Sudbury, skilled trades power our economy, but we need to ensure that young people see the trades as a viable career choice. We know we cannot build strong without a skilled workforce.

I invite everyone to join me tonight at a reception hosted by the Pearson Centre and Skills Canada at the National Arts Centre, where featured guests will share their insights on how to engage young people in the trades.

Mr. Speaker, what could a six-year-old boy's birthday teach us about the struggles facing Canadian families? This weekend, we took our grandson to Canadian Tire to buy his birthday present. I saw his little eyes light up as he picked out his hockey stick, helmet and gloves. He could hardly wait to get home.

There we were, out on the street, Grandma in goal and David's little legs racing after the ball, shouting “goal” every time he got one past me. It was such a simple and wonderful afternoon. Later, around the dinner table, the conversation changed. My daughter talked about how even these little extras were becoming difficult to afford. My son-in-law, a schoolteacher, told us that his total mortgage cost had just increased by $6,000 following last week's interest rate hike.

How many young families are having these same conversations around the dinner table? They are making difficult choices to live within their means, while the Prime Minister continues running massive deficits, with inflation eating away at their paycheques. Why must Canadians live within their means when the government refuses to do the same?

Mr. Speaker, I want to acknowledge the tireless work of Dr. Anas Al-Kassem. A surgeon, Dr. Al-Kassem came to Canada to complete his medical residency. When he was about to return to Syria in 2011, war broke out in his country. He then decided he could be more useful to Syrians by organizing relief efforts from Canada.

Along with two colleagues, he founded UOSSM, the Union of Medical Care and Relief Organizations, with the goal of providing much-needed medicine and equipment to hospitals under constant bombing and overwhelmed with a war that went on for 15 years. He personally carried out around 20 humanitarian missions in Syria, operating on hundreds of trauma patients at Bab-al Hawa and many other underground hospitals, even as doctors and medical staff were being targeted by the Bashar al-Assad government.
Dr. Al-Kassem is a great humanitarian and a true Canadian hero.

Mr. Speaker, a few weeks ago, as Kol Nidrei began at the Sons of Jacob Synagogue in Belleville, a gunman arrived with a shotgun, explosives and a plan. Inside, about two dozen people had gathered to ask for forgiveness on the holiest night of the year. When the shots rang out, they pushed the tables together and lay on the floor, not knowing if the doors would hold. They held because of two constables, not policy: Jeff Smith was shot multiple times, and he kept fighting, and Michael McCurdy ran toward gunfire to stand beside him. Constable Smith just came home from the hospital.

Because of them, those families are here with us in Ottawa today. They came to remind us that hatred does not happen to faceless strangers. It happens to neighbours in small cities, people who came only to pray.

No one should need to arm guards to worship in Canada, and meeting the rising tide of extremism means acting before the next congregation hits the floor to listen. We will keep saying it until the last person with the power to act finally does.

Mr. Speaker, today I want to recognize members of the Intentional Community Consortium who are in Ottawa for their annual day on the Hill. Representing 85 agencies across Ontario and Quebec, the ICC is celebrating its 10th anniversary. That is 10 years of advocating for supportive housing solutions for individuals with developmental disabilities across Canada.

Earlier this fall, we celebrated the opening of the Frankfort Family Reena Residence in the heart of my riding of Eglinton—Lawrence with chair Gary Gladstone.
