Because of the $44 million in funding from Canada's government, that project has delivered 111 new affordable units, giving 168 people with diverse needs a place to call home.

I would like to thank the Intentional Community Consortium for the important work it does to build stronger, more accessible communities, and I invite all hon. members to join us in the Speaker's dining room following question period.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Pierre Poilievre (Leader of the Opposition, CPC):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, the number one priority in the budget must be to save Canadians money. Saving Canadians money is essential because, after 10 years, the Liberals have driven up the price of gas, groceries and homes.
The quickest way to reverse this inflation is to eliminate all gas taxes. Eliminating all gas taxes would cut the cost of gas by 20¢ a litre and save every family $1,000.
Will the Prime Minister accept our idea to save Canadians money?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Julie Dabrusin (Minister of the Environment, Climate Change and Nature, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, we are working hard on affordability for Canadians. One example is the heat pump program, which will help Canadians across the country lower the cost of heating their homes.

I also want to talk about opportunities, because everyone wants to have a good job. People in the member's riding are benefiting from biodiesel and canola subsidies. Farmers in his community will make more money thanks to what we are doing for that region.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Pierre Poilievre (Leader of the Opposition, CPC):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, heat pump subsidies may be helping Brookfield, the Prime Minister's company, which invested in that. Biodiesel subsidies paid for by Canadian taxpayers are going to American companies.
The top priority should be to save Canadians money by eliminating all taxes starting now until July. That will also lower the cost of all the products arriving by truck.
Why does the Prime Minister insist on taxing Canadians, who cannot pay more?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Julie Dabrusin (Minister of the Environment, Climate Change and Nature, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, why is the member not interested in working for the farmers in his riding?

Imperial is currently producing biodiesel at the Strathcona refinery. It uses 50% of Alberta's canola. The member represents a riding that produces a great deal of canola. It makes a lot of sense to carry on with what we are doing. It is helping his constituents.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Pierre Poilievre (Leader of the Opposition, CPC):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, job one for the budget is very simple: save Canadians money. It needs to save Canadians money on their groceries, save Canadians money at the pump and save them money on the materials that go into building homes. The fastest way to save Canadians money is to get rid of all taxes on gas, get rid of the so-called fuel standard tax and the GST on gas and diesel, and get rid of the excise tax until Canada Day.
Will the Prime Minister accept our idea to save Canadians money by axing taxes on gas?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Julie Dabrusin (Minister of the Environment, Climate Change and Nature, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I will say it once again, because it is so astonishing. The member opposite represents the second-largest canola-producing riding in Alberta, has a canola crusher in his riding and is right adjacent to Imperial Oil's Strathcona refinery, which actually produces biodiesel supported by the clean fuel regulations. This is good for canola farmers across our country. It is good for his own constituents, and I would hope that he would stand up with them.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Pierre Poilievre (Leader of the Opposition, CPC):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, it is no wonder Canadians are out of money. The Liberal government is out of touch. Yes, the farmers in my riding say the single biggest expense this year is the cost of diesel. Some of them are spending $25,000 or $30,000 on diesel. One farmer spends $5,000 a day during the harvest. All of it gets passed on in higher food costs. The Liberal government continues to add 20¢ a litre in taxes. The best way to save Canadians money is to scrap all those taxes.
Will the government accept our idea to save farmers, small businesses, seniors and Canadians money?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Wayne Long (Secretary of State (Canada Revenue Agency and Financial Institutions), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I have great news for Canadians and great news for that party across the House. On Thursday, we will table our second generational budget, budget 2026. We will build Canada strong. We will invest in our country from coast to coast to coast. We will make sure nobody is left behind. We will continue with the groceries and essentials benefit and fight for affordability measures for Canadians. On this side of the House, we deliver on affordability. They continue with the rhetoric.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Pierre Poilievre (Leader of the Opposition, CPC:

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, this will be their second generational budget in one year. Canadians cannot afford another generation of Liberal taxes. They are out of money. The member is out of touch to say they have delivered on affordability when food bank demand is up 9% year over year, with 2.35 million record-smashing visits to the food bank and the largest number of people who cannot believe they will never be able to afford a home is in this country, of any of the 22 countries polled by Habitat for Humanity.
Why will they not stop wasting time and save Canadians money?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Wayne Long (Secretary of State (Canada Revenue Agency and Financial Institutions), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, as always, on that side of the House, it is hands up, no plan and no focus. There is nothing on that side of the House.

On this side of the House, we are going to table budget 2026. We are masters of our own destiny. We are going to build Canada strong. We are going to build a strong, resilient economy. We are going to invest and build Canada while looking after those who need help the most. We just paused the excise tax on fuel.
We are going to continue to deliver affordability measures for Canadians. That side continues with nothing.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Pierre Poilievre (Leader of the Opposition, CPC):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, the member had trouble following what is a very clear and direct path to make life affordable. The shortest distance between two points is a straight line, and the straight line is this. They get rid of all taxes on gas and immediately start saving people 20¢ a litre. They cancel the reinstallation of the excise tax and it goes up to almost 30¢ a litre. That will save a Canadian family $1,200. This is an immediate action the government can take to save money for Canadians.
Will it do it in the budget?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Tim Hodgson (Minister of Energy and Natural Resources, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, let me help the member opposite. He could have voted for the groceries and essentials benefit and saved a family of four $1,900. He could have voted for the child benefit and saved families $7,000 a year. He could have voted for child care and saved families $16,000 a year. He could have voted for a tax cut and saved families another $840 a year.
He voted against every single one of those affordability measures. We will take no lessons from him on affordability.

Mr. Speaker, Canada and the European Union have announced initiatives that may, or may not, lead to associate membership status. They discussed critical minerals, energy, regulatory alignment in trade, cultural exchanges, wildfire management and much more. All these areas fall under Quebec's jurisdiction. Not only does the federal government lack the constitutional authority to act in these areas, but it will also be unable to fulfill its commitments without Quebec's support.
Moving forward, will the federal government ensure that Quebec has a direct seat at the negotiating table?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Steven MacKinnon (Minister of Transport and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, Quebeckers, like all Canadians, are very proud that we are moving forward toward a much more structured and much deeper relationship and, yes, toward diversifying our trade beyond our dependence on the United States.

I believe that Quebeckers can look forward to a much more promising and prosperous future in which we collaborate with our European counterparts in a wide range of areas. This is good for Quebec, and it is good for Canada.

Mr. Speaker, the federal government is discussing a potentially major agreement with Europe that would cover areas where it has no jurisdiction. The government never asked Quebec for its opinion, the Liberals never consulted the public in an election, and there was never a debate in Parliament. Everything is happening behind the Prime Minister's closed doors. This matter is important enough to warrant at least basic transparency.
Will the government convene a debate in the House this week?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Steven MacKinnon (Minister of Transport and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, it is hard to be more transparent than holding a meeting in Montreal in front of all stakeholders, including six former premiers of the province of Quebec.
We are obviously delighted to have Quebec and society as a whole involved in the talks. The discussions began in Montreal, and they will of course continue.
We will continue to be totally transparent as we sign very promising agreements with the European Union.

Mr. Speaker, excluding Quebec from the discussions with Europe is not the right approach. The Prime Minister said that he recognizes doctrines that work. Well, the Gérin‑Lajoie doctrine works. That is how Quebec got its own seat at the Organisation internationale de la Francophonie. It is how Quebec was able to negotiate a carbon market with California. It is how Quebec got a seat at the table for the negotiations leading to the free trade agreement with Europe.
Since it works, will the Government of Canada officially recognize the Gérin‑Lajoie doctrine today?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Steven MacKinnon (Minister of Transport and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, we will of course continue to consult Quebec and all the provinces on matters within their areas of jurisdiction, including workforce training, portability, procurement and all things labour. We will certainly continue to initiate and pursue discussions with all the provinces on matters that fall within their jurisdiction and capabilities.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister stood in the House and said affordability is the best it has been in decades, and we know that is not true. The government said that the debt-to-GDP would go down, and we know that is not true. After a decade of runaway Liberal spending, Canadians cannot keep up. Food banks saw a record 2.35 million visits in a single month, and inflation is above the bank's target range. Instead of easing the pressure, Ottawa keeps adding to it. Federal taxes still add up to about 20¢ for every litre of gas.
Nobody is telling the Prime Minister to change things that are out of his control. He found billions for everything else. Will he find 20¢ a litre for every Canadian on Thursday?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Ryan Turnbull (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance and National Revenue and to the Secretary of State (Canada Revenue Agency and Financial Institutions), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, we can all recognize that Canada has the strongest fiscal position in the G7. We have the lowest net debt-to-GDP ratio by far, given it is at 40.7%, with the G7 average, excluding Canada, at over 100%. We found $60 billion in savings, and we are on track to balance the operating budget one year ahead of schedule. Also, we topped the G7 in second quarter growth and have seen a large spike in new business investment.
Our plan is working, and budget 2026 will build on that plan to build the strongest economy in the G7. Just wait until Thursday.

Mr. Speaker, I think he read the wrong piece of paper. That was not at all my question. Pausing one tax until January is not relief for Canadians. Canadians need to work and eat all year round. Relief for a portion of the tax for a portion of the year, as the Liberals pad their coffers with windfall profits from the high price of oil, is not actually relief for families.
The only thing standing between Canadians and saving them money is political will, so I will ask again slowly: Will he find 20¢ a litre for every Canadian on Thursday?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Ryan Turnbull (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance and National Revenue and to the Secretary of State (Canada Revenue Agency and Financial Institutions), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, let me say it slowly. We know the economy is going through shocks, tariffs and energy price shocks, and we know that that has put pressure on Canadian households.

Unlike the opposition, who are only full of manufactured outrage, we are actually doing things to help Canadian families. We cut income tax for 22 million Canadians, suspended the excise tax on fuel, introduced the groceries and essentials benefit and cut taxes on new home purchases, saving families up to $50,000 right across the country. That is how we help Canadians with affordability. It is not by claiming we care and then opposing every possible solution in the House.

Mr. Speaker, the out-of-touch Liberal Prime Minister said affordability is the best it has been in a decade. I would say that too if I owned shares in Brookfield. While he is hiking gas taxes, families are struggling with whether they can afford groceries or gas this week. We know the Prime Minister does not control world prices, but he does control Liberal taxes on gas, like the clean fuel standard and the excise tax, and the GST on top of that.
Will the Liberals listen to Conservatives and remove all federal fuel taxes off gas in their upcoming budget this week, yes or no?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Leslie Church (Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretaries of State for Labour, for Seniors, and for Children and Youth, and to the Minister of Jobs and Families (Persons with Disabilities), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, this is the government that, from day one, has cut taxes for more than 22 million Canadians and reduced the fuel excise tax on Canadians as well. Despite the uncertainty that our economy is facing, GDP growth picked up earlier this year and is going to continue next year. The Bank of Canada expects growth to increase as a result of the government's measures, measures such as our productivity mega deduction, investment in major projects and business investment that is at its highest in 20 years. This is part of an economic plan for Canadians that is building prosperity, building growth and creating jobs. It is going to help that member and his constituents every step of the way.
Mr. Speaker, stalling the economy for two quarters is success to these guys. I would hate to see what failure looks like.

Canadians want relief at the pump right now. Conservatives know every dollar that Canadians save at the pump on gas means more money that they can spend on groceries. That is why Conservatives are calling on this incompetent Liberal government to remove all Liberal fuel taxes off gas, including the clean fuel standard, the excise tax and the GST.
Will the Liberals grow some compassion and do it, yes or no?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Leslie Church (Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretaries of State for Labour, for Seniors, and for Children and Youth, and to the Minister of Jobs and Families (Persons with Disabilities), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I cannot help but pick up on that member's comment about compassion.

I will talk about compassion. Compassion is a national school food program that is available in 63 public school jurisdictions in that member's province, a program that helps nearly 60,000 kids not go hungry at school. That is compassion. That is what this government stands for, and what we are going to continue to deliver every single day.

Mr. Speaker, a tax on gas is a tax on everything. It is a tax on driving to work. It is a tax on getting groceries to the store. Despite the Prime Minister's claims that affordability is the best it has been in over a decade, ordinary Canadians are feeling the pinch. Necessities of life are starting to feel like luxuries.
The government can control taxes. It can take all federal taxes off fuel, and it can do it on Thursday. Will it?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Adam van Koeverden (Secretary of State (Sport), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, Canadians watching back home must think this is question period rerun hour, because the Conservative leader is back on his “axe the tax, no facts” rhetoric. It did not work three years ago.

We removed the taxes on fuel, removed taxes on housing and reduced income taxes. As a result, families and farmers are experiencing a little bit of relief. The Conservatives voted against all of those measures. Why does the Conservative leader not come clean with Canadians and tell them how he plans to pay for his empty promises? Canadians have already made up their mind on how their plan is going to affect their pocketbooks. They voted against it.
Mr. Speaker, Canadians back home are well aware that this is not called “answer period”, and that secretary of state has demonstrated exactly why.

The only people better off in this Canada, with these Liberal budgets, are the Prime Minister's banker buddies. The interest on the debt is $58.7 billion. Now that is money spent on nothing. That could build 60 hospitals. That could build 120,000 housing units. That could give tax relief to Canadians of $6,000.
Why are the only ones who are getting ahead the Prime Minister's buddies?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Adam van Koeverden (Secretary of State (Sport), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, once again, I implore the Conservatives to tell Canadians how they plan to pay for all of these empty promises.

I have a couple of ideas, though. They have already said that they are going to cut the Canadian child benefit. They already said they are not a fan of the groceries and essentials benefit. They already said that affordable housing is too Soviet for them. Perhaps they will do what they did when they were in government, which was to cut funding for veterans affairs offices and reduce the support that they give to veterans.
Canadians are well aware of what the Conservatives have in store for them.

Mr. Speaker, the Bank of Canada forecasts that growth will be just 1% in Canada in 2026, compared to 3% globally. Half of this meagre growth comes from government spending. This shows just how much our businesses are struggling. Under the Liberals, the economy is idling, and it is workers who are paying the price. On Thursday, the Liberal Prime Minister will have a choice to make: keep spending, or leave more money in Canadians' pockets. That same Liberal Prime Minister once promised to reduce the debt-to-GDP ratio.
Will he keep his promise?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Nathalie Provost (Secretary of State (Nature), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I thank my kind colleague for the question.

We have been working to boost Canadians' purchasing power for a year now. In the upcoming budget, we will continue to pursue this vision because it is clear that Canadians need help and support. We need to boost their economic well-being. That is the purpose of our programs, such as the groceries benefit and dental care for children. These are the kinds of measures that our colleagues do not support. I am curious to see what the budget holds. We will help Canadians even more.

Mr. Speaker, the entire planet is wondering how to use AI while keeping the environment in mind, given that data centres consume huge quantities of water and energy. Well, it is not the entire planet. One country of die-hard polluters still holds out against the modern era. That country is Canada. Seeing the immense amount of energy that data centres need, Canada has decided that if it builds data centres in Alberta, it would be able to power them with gas. Imagine how much gas will be sold.
Is there anything the Liberals do not view as an opportunity to sell more oil and gas?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Julie Dabrusin (Minister of the Environment, Climate Change and Nature, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, when we talk about energy, we are talking about clean energy. What are we doing? We are making sure that we will continue to have a large electricity grid. We are going to double its capacity by 2050.
When it comes to AI, it is fair to say that we have put guidelines in place to clearly explain how we are going to work hard to ensure that we can protect Canadians while maintaining AI sovereignty.

Mr. Speaker, seriously, a researcher at Utah State University calculated the potential emissions from a mammoth data centre in Grande Prairie, Alberta. That one centre would release the equivalent of 23 Hiroshima atom bombs of heat waste every day. It is not easy to reconcile that with the fight against climate change.

The Liberals look at projects like that and their first thought is that they could power them with gas. Only a Liberal could come up with such a lousy idea. Are they deliberately trying to sabotage their climate targets?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Steven MacKinnon (Minister of Transport and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, if the Bloc Québécois cares about greenhouse gas emissions and their effects on the environment, I have good news for its members: They have an opportunity to support the most transformative emissions-reducing project of all, a project that would revolutionize mobility in Quebec while generating 51,000 jobs and several points of GDP, not to mention sales tax revenues for the province. I am talking about the high-speed rail project that will run from Quebec City to Trois‑Rivières, Laval, Montreal and Gatineau.

Mr. Speaker, Toronto was horrified by the Bridle Path home invasion in which a father and two daughters were shot and a mother injured. This was the 119th invasion in Toronto this year. That is a 32% increase from the same period in 2025.

It is clear that the Liberal government's bail and sentencing reform is a failure. The bail principle of restraint, to let an accused out at the earliest opportunity, remains. Conservatives wanted mandatory minimum sentences for armed home invasions. Instead the Liberals gutted all mandatory minimum sentences.
Will the Attorney General own his failure and work with Conservatives to pass real bail and sentencing reform?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Sean Fraser (Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada and Minister responsible for the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, we had a choice of who to listen to when it came to actually developing measures that were going to promote public safety in this country: Conservative members, who would simply yell and make noise on the floor of the House of Commons, or those who have dedicated their lives and careers to demand better public safety outcomes for Canadians.

We chose to work with police who work on the ground to improve public safety. We chose to work with provincial governments that have the responsibility to administer the justice system of their province, and we worked with advocacy organizations that defended the interests of victims. I think we made the right choice.

Mr. Speaker, according to the Toronto Star, home invasions are up 50% in Toronto. Canadians want action. That is why we have two bills before the House. We have the proposed safe at home act, which would create a stand-alone offence for home invasions and carry with it a mandatory minimum of five years and a maximum of life imprisonment. We also have the proposed stand on guard law, which would strengthen provisions for self-defence so Canadians can defend themselves in their own home.
I have a very simple question for the minister. On these two bills, will the Liberals stand with us and support them so that we can protect Canadians in their own home, yes or no?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Sean Fraser (Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada and Minister responsible for the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, protecting the ability of Canadians to defend themselves in their own home is absolutely a priority that we share. Thankfully, that is what the law provides for today, but we took it a step further by implementing changes to the Criminal Code, which are now the law of Canada, that ensure there is a reverse onus when we have violent home invasions for someone seeking to have bail. It ensures that there is potential for tougher sentences when there are violent home invasions, particularly when they are tied to organized crime.

We are seized with the issue. We are working, and as a result of the measures we put in place, we are seeing progress across the country. The job is not done, but we are trending in the right direction.
Mr. Speaker, I cannot understand for the life of me why the minister cannot answer the very simple question.

The father of the family who just suffered the violent home invasion in Toronto said the following: “It is difficult to put into words the trauma of experiencing something so horrific in the one place where everyone should feel safest: their own home.” That is why we put these two bills before the House.
This is a very simple question. Canadians deserve a very clear answer. Will the Liberals support these two pieces of legislation that we have before the House so we can protect Canadians, yes or no?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Gary Anandasangaree (Minister of Public Safety, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, first of all, we send our deepest condolences to the family impacted by this horrific incident. All of us in this House share the need for safety and security in someone's home.

However, I will be very clear: We brought forward significant legislation, the most comprehensive criminal justice legislation in a generation, including stronger sentencing as well as bail reform and including protection of victims' rights. These are critical pieces of legislation that will ensure the safety and security of Canadians over the long term.

Mr. Speaker, recently a Toronto family of four was terrorized by three masked men who entered their home with hammers and guns. Three people were shot and two people were hit with hammers. The family will never be the same. People should feel that they are safest when they are in their homes. Therefore, will the Prime Minister support our legislation to get tough on home invaders so people can feel safest in their homes?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Gary Anandasangaree (Minister of Public Safety, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, we have brought forward transformational legislation to protect those who are suffering from the scourge of issues such as home invasion. We have in place Bill C-14, which strengthens bail as well as sentencing. We have Bill C-16, which ensures victims' rights are protected. These are transformational pieces of legislation. Unfortunately, the party opposite did not give us its support. It is important that these pieces of legislation are implemented and that is what we look to the provinces to do.
Mr. Speaker, the minister speaks about transformational legislation. The Liberals can tell that to the family of four who are now in the hospital.

We have to ensure that people are safest when the are in their own homes. Reforms are absolutely needed. One of the answers is our safe at home act that was put forward by the member for Vaughan—Woodbridge.
How many more families need to suffer in their own homes before the Liberals take the time to act?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Gary Anandasangaree (Minister of Public Safety, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I repeat: We have brought forward significant legislation that will protect Canadians in their homes and on the streets, as well as those victims who have been impacted by the criminal justice system. What we need right now is collaboration from the opposition. We do not need piecemeal pieces of a private member's bill that does not look at the bigger picture. That is why we have brought forward the most comprehensive criminal justice legislation in a generation.

Mr. Speaker, every year, 1,600 families face the unimaginable tragedy of the loss of a child while on parental leave. Last week, this House unanimously passed Evan's law, which would allow those affected to maintain their parental benefits while reducing unnecessary red tape. It is something that members from all parties have worked towards, and I thank everyone in this House and outside it for their efforts in making this happen.
Could the Secretary of State for Labour comment on the impact of this legislation and the importance of implementing it as soon as possible?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. John Zerucelli (Secretary of State (Labour), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I want to thank my colleague from Burnaby North—Seymour for his advocacy on this very important piece of legislation. No parent should have to navigate government red tape while grieving the loss of a child. That is why we are moving quickly on Bill C-222 to ensure grieving parents can continue receiving their parental benefits without unnecessary paperwork and administrative burdens. When parents experience unimaginable loss, they deserve compassion, financial stability and the time and space to grieve.

Mr. Speaker, the Auditor General released a scathing report on the Liberal government's mismanagement of Canada's emergency medical stockpile. These supplies are critical to saving lives during pandemics, natural disasters and nuclear emergencies, and yet for years the Liberals have not known what supplies Canada needs, how to manage what we have or how to coordinate with provinces. They have wasted hundreds of millions of tax dollars. This mismanagement poses a serious risk to our national security.
The Liberals have governed for over 10 years, including during a pandemic. When are they planning to fix these problems?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Marjorie Michel (Minister of Health, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank my colleague for her question. Once again, I would like to assure her that the Public Health Agency of Canada is ready to deal with any future challenges. One of the reasons I can say this is that we were able to fulfill 81 requests from the provinces. The stock levels in the warehouses were normal. Yes, some masks went to waste, but that is bound to happen from time to time.

Mr. Speaker, safeguarding Canadians is the fundamental responsibility of the federal government and yet this Auditor General report reveals that the Liberals are failing at basic governance. They threw out over $300 million of medical supplies that could have been used at our local hospitals before they expired. Another $20 million of critical pharmaceuticals were destroyed because somebody left a freezer open. The Liberals have known about these problems for years.
What is it going to take for that minister and the Liberal government to deliver basic governance on emergency management? What is it going to—
The hon. Minister of Health.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Marjorie Michel (Minister of Health, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I want my colleague to know that we learned lessons from the pandemic and that we are prepared. Of course, we will occasionally have to deal with the fact that certain products have to be discarded because they have reached their expiry date. However, we are prepared and will be ready to meet the needs of Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, steelworkers are losing their jobs. Four in 10 manufacturers have moved production south or plan to. That will mean over 100,000 jobs lost in two months. Those workers cannot wait another two and a half years for a deal.
Will the Prime Minister deliver a better deal than he was looking at in August or should we be waiting for the next public opinion poll to find out what a good deal is?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Dominic LeBlanc (President of the King’s Privy Council for Canada and Minister responsible for Canada-U.S. Trade, Intergovernmental Affairs, Internal Trade, and One Canadian Economy, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I think our colleague on the other side of the House is confusing our government with the weak-kneed approach of the Conservative Party in dealing with the Americans. We know they would have accepted any deal at any time to just get a deal that would not be in the interest of Canadian workers, the Canadian economy or the sovereignty of our country.
We are going to do that difficult work that is necessary to protect our economy, and when that deal is available we will accept it.

Mr. Speaker, what is weak-kneed is concession after concession for over a year and a half, rather than building the strength of this country. Two straight months of zero growth and now the economy is shrinking. Parents are skipping meals so their kids can eat. We have another $733 billion of debt, with $6,000 per family just to pay the interest. Canadians did not elect a performer. They were promised a negotiator.
Will the Prime Minister finally get the great deal he promised, or will this just be another month of political theatre while Canadians suffer?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Dominic LeBlanc (President of the King’s Privy Council for Canada and Minister responsible for Canada-U.S. Trade, Intergovernmental Affairs, Internal Trade, and One Canadian Economy, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, we understand that Canadian businesses and Canadian workers are facing extraordinary pressure because of these unjustified and illegal tariffs, unlike the Conservatives who resisted our government's strong decision to put in place retaliatory measures to protect sectors of our economy facing these unfair tariffs.
Our government has said we will do whatever it takes for as long as it takes to protect Canadian workers but we are also talking to the Americans about getting the right deal for Canada.

Mr. Speaker, last week the Prime Minister said he was prepared to wait out the President for two years. Then he suddenly called six by-elections and suddenly getting a deal with the Americans is back on the agenda. As a member of the gill caucus, I can tell members that a fish out of water flip-flops less than the Prime Minister.
Canadians were promised a master negotiator. When will he put Canadian jobs ahead of his political agenda, or are Canadian workers simply pawns in these by-election campaigns?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Dominic LeBlanc (President of the King’s Privy Council for Canada and Minister responsible for Canada-U.S. Trade, Intergovernmental Affairs, Internal Trade, and One Canadian Economy, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I was Minister of Fisheries and Oceans for two years. I understand what a fish out of water looks like. Mr. Speaker, perhaps if you look to your left, you might have seen one.

However, what is important is that all Canadians know, even the Conservatives should acknowledge, that our government will do everything it takes for as long as it takes to support Canadian workers and Canadian businesses facing these unfair and illegal tariffs. Yes, we will talk to the Americans and we will do the hard work necessary to get the right deal for Canada and Canadian workers.

Mr. Speaker, the economy has stalled with two straight months of zero growth and now it is shrinking. Manufacturers are packing up and heading south. Four in 10 have already moved production to the United States or are planning to. Stelco workers are still out of a job. Last week, the Prime Minister said he could wait two and a half more years without a trade deal. This week, he called the by-elections and he announced he is ready to start talks again.
Will the Prime Minister finally get the deal he promised or will this just be another month of political theatre?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Carlos Leitão (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, the deal we will get will be the right deal for Canada, not just any deal. Our first priority has always been the future and well-being of Canadian workers.

As for Stelco and all the other steel companies around, we will continue to support and work with companies that believe in Canada and that continue to invest in Canada. As for those that do not, we will not support them. By the way, there are five days left for Stelco.

Mr. Speaker, here are some facts: Homebuilding is down, food bank lineups are up and growth has flatlined. Now the great economist has broken his own fiscal anchors, piling on more national debt. This is the debt that our children will have to pay.
The Prime Minister promised Canadians a great deal. He said he was the man to deliver it, and we are still waiting.
He calls the by-elections, and then he calls Trump, so I will ask this again: Will the Prime Minister finally get the deal he promised, or is this just some more by-election political theatre?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Ryan Turnbull (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance and National Revenue and to the Secretary of State (Canada Revenue Agency and Financial Institutions), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, we will not take lessons from the Conservatives on political theatre, because that is all they do in the House.

We are standing up to support Canadians. Conservatives can promote falsehoods all they want and string as many of them together as they want, but they do not constitute a truth. We have cut taxes on income, housing, fuel and new business investment. We have saved over $60 billion on government operations. We have the strongest fiscal position in the G7 and topped the G7 in the second quarter in terms of GDP growth. We have seen a spike in new business and foreign direct investment, and we have used our fiscal space to help Canadians—
The hon. member for Charlesbourg—Haute-Saint-Charles.
Mr. Speaker, in Canada, the economy is in decline and food banks are overwhelmed. The Prime Minister is using an old trick to try to cover up his failures: He is creating a smokescreen.

Last week, he said that he could wait two and a half more years without a deal with Donald Trump. On the weekend, he called six by-elections, and then what did he do? He picked up the phone and called his good friend Donald. Then, he announced that he is resuming negotiations. That is quite the coincidence. This is another political diversion tactic.
My question is this: Does the Prime Minister actually think that he can fix the trade issues with Donald Trump, or is this just another smokescreen to sway voters?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Dominic LeBlanc (President of the King’s Privy Council for Canada and Minister responsible for Canada-U.S. Trade, Intergovernmental Affairs, Internal Trade, and One Canadian Economy, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I understand that our Conservative friends are worried about the by-elections, and with good reason. I think it is important to note that nothing has changed since last week. We obviously called by-elections because these ridings need people to represent them in the House. The reason we are holding these by-elections is because members of the Conservative caucus have stepped down.
At the same time, yes, we are having conversations with our American counterparts, and we will continue to work until we have an agreement that is in Canada's best interests.
Mr. Speaker, we are starting to figure out their tricks.

Last summer, the government was about to reach an agreement, but just before the election and the advance voting for the by-elections, it suddenly withdrew from the negotiations. What did that do? It influenced the public, who was afraid of Donald Trump.
Now, six by-elections are coming up, and what is the government doing? It is calling its friend Donald and saying that it wants to negotiate.
What is that if not a way to influence voters through twisted political games?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Dominic LeBlanc (President of the King’s Privy Council for Canada and Minister responsible for Canada-U.S. Trade, Intergovernmental Affairs, Internal Trade, and One Canadian Economy, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I understand that our Conservative friends are afraid of the by-elections. I have said this before. By the way, it was their members who triggered some of these by-elections by leaving their caucus. We hope that voters in those ridings have an opportunity to elect strong members to this Parliament.

At the same time, yes, we are working with our American counterparts. We are trying to get the unjustified and illegal tariffs removed. We are also supporting Canadian industries with our friends in the provincial governments.
That is what a responsible government does.

Mr. Speaker, for too long, we have waited until men and boys reached a crisis point before offering them help. In February, the Minister of Health took an important step toward addressing this issue by launching a national conversation on men and boys' health.
With International Men's Day approaching on November 19, can the minister tell us what the next steps will be in developing Canada's brand new men and boys' health strategy?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Marjorie Michel (Minister of Health, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank my colleague for his question. Today, we released the “What We Heard” report on our national conversation on men and boys' health. Nearly 6,000 Canadians and numerous organizations from across the country shared their perspectives. These contributions will help shape Canada's first-ever men and boys' health strategy. This strategy is intended to improve well-being not only for men and boys, but for all communities and all Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister vowed to make Canada its own best customer. He promised that when his government spends, it will select Canadian suppliers and Canadian jobs first. When it comes to election time, the Prime Minister is elbows up, but when it comes to contract time, he chooses America first.

He awarded a U.S. security firm with ties to Trump's ICE a $12-million contract over the Canadian Corps of Commissionaires, the largest employer of veterans in Canada. Why did the Prime Minister sacrifice Canadian veterans' jobs to put America first?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Jenna Sudds (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Government Transformation, Public Works and Procurement and to the Secretary of State (Defence Procurement), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, our priority is to put Canadian content, Canadian companies and Canadian workers first, and to use our purchasing power to grow production here at home. That is companies contributing substantively to our economy, employing people, creating good jobs here in our communities and paying taxes here in our communities. That is what we are doing to build Canada strong and build Canadian innovation.
Mr. Speaker, actions speak louder than words, and the government did exactly the opposite of what the member just said.

The Canadian Corps of Commissionaires is a not-for-profit that prioritizes the hiring of Canada's veterans. For generations, the Canadian government has provided it the right of first refusal for security contracts. The Commissionaires put in a competitive bid, but the America-first Prime Minister chose Trump's favourite security contractor, Allied Universal, for the job.
Was this yet another concession by the Liberal government? Why is the Prime Minister putting the interests of American corporate profits over job opportunities for our courageous veterans?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Jenna Sudds (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Government Transformation, Public Works and Procurement and to the Secretary of State (Defence Procurement), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, on this side of the House, we are working hard to attract more investment into our country, investment that delivers tangible results and lasting benefits to Canadian communities and supply chains.
They want to talk about results. I point them to the contracts that have been awarded. I look at General Dynamics as an example—
Some hon. members: Oh, oh!
I let it go as long as I could.
The hon. member may continue.

Mr. Speaker, as I was saying, we can point to the results and the impact that this policy has been having already in just a few months. We have seen, most recently, a contract awarded to General Dynamics.
Those are tangible results. Those are jobs in communities that matter to Canadians.
Mr. Speaker, the Commissionaires is a not-for-profit organization, Canada's largest private sector employer of veterans. What commissionaires earn goes back to veterans, not shareholders.

Justin Trudeau once told veterans that they were asking for more than he was able to give. That was a slap in the face. Now the Liberal government has handed a CRA security contract to Allied Universal, an American company tied to Trump's ICE deportation machine, just to save $80,000. That is a backhand to the face.
When will the Prime Minister stop beating down on veterans?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Jill McKnight (Minister of Veterans Affairs and Associate Minister of National Defence, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I thank my colleague for his military service and for raising his concerns.

Let me be clear again. Veterans Affairs Canada does not award guard services contracts on behalf of other departments or agencies. I, of course, share the view that we must ensure that veterans have the right opportunities to find rewarding employment of their choosing when they are ready. It is fundamental to the national veterans employment strategy.
Our government has worked with and will continue to work with veteran employers as we build the strongest economy in the G7.

Mr. Speaker, Canada has not recognized any conflict since Korea as wartime service, despite the fact that veterans of the Persian Gulf, Afghanistan and other conflicts participated in operations that can only be described as war. This reality must be recognized. Too many veterans and their families do not see their hardship and sacrifice reflected by the term “special duty service”.
Can the minister tell the House what the government is doing to recognize wartime service?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Jill McKnight (Minister of Veterans Affairs and Associate Minister of National Defence, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I support my colleague's dedication to advancing this important matter. I also want to recognize the parliamentarians who served our country in uniform.

Canada must ensure that the recognition of service and sacrifice reflects the evolving nature of military service. Meaningful recognition must honour those who have served, reflect our diverse military history and inspire future generations.
In the coming months, consultations with veterans, serving members, historians and experts will ensure we get this right. The work has started, and we look forward to sharing more in due course.

Mr. Speaker, a recent government decision under the non-insured health benefits program is limiting access to mental health services in Lloydminster, Canada's only border city. Councillors have been told they can no longer serve indigenous patients because of where their clinic is located in the city and their provincial registration. For patients, many of whom are residential and day school survivors, losing an established therapeutic relationship is deeply disruptive.
Will the minister cut this red tape to ensure that indigenous patients can continue to access the care they need in the city where they live?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Mandy Gull-Masty (Minister of Indigenous Services, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, this critical service is available, but we want to be sure that service providers are able to respond to clients' needs, whether they are living in a city or providing a service from another province. We want to be sure that they are able to provide the best and most adequate service to the clients who are going to them and that they are able to be served in the spaces they live in.
If my colleague wants to work together, I am more than willing to give her the answers she needs for her riding.

Mr. Speaker, workers and their families need good, safe, rewarding jobs across Canada. In the construction sector, these jobs come from unionized companies powered by skilled labour. The government can support them by requiring labour agreements on all taxpayer-funded infrastructure projects. This is smart economics. Productivity from unionized labour is 17% higher than for open-shop contractors.
Will the Liberals mandate project labour agreements for all infrastructure deals to generate the high-quality results that unionized building trades deliver?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. John Zerucelli (Secretary of State (Labour), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I know that the BC Building Trades is in Ottawa this week, and I welcome it here.

We are building right across this country. We are building with Canadian steel, Canadian lumber and Canadian unionized workers. Nowhere do we see this building more than in British Columbia with LNG one and LNG two.
We are going to stand up for our unionized workers. I was proud to announce $420 million under the union training and innovation program, which will support union training centres.
We are building this country. I hope the member joins us.

Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to present, in both official languages, the 10th report of the Standing Committee on Environment and Sustainable Development, entitled “Statutory Review of the Canadian Net-Zero Emissions Accountability Act”.

Mr. Speaker. I have the honour to present, in both official languages, the ninth report of the Standing Committee on Justice and Human Rights in relation to Bill S-233, an act to amend the Criminal Code, assault against persons who provide health services and first responders.
The committee requests an extension.

Pursuant to Standing Order 97.1(3)(a), a motion to concur in the report is deemed moved, the question deemed put and a recorded division deemed requested and deferred until Wednesday, November 4, at the expiry of the time provided for Oral Questions.
moved that Bill S-214, An Act to amend the Special Economic Measures Act (disposal of foreign state assets), be read the first time.

Mr. Speaker, today I am honoured to introduce Bill S-214, an act that would amend the Special Economic Measures Act, SEMA, regarding the disposal of foreign state assets. This enactment would amend the Special Economic Measures Act to allow the Governor in Council to dispose of a foreign state's assets seized under the act if the seizure occurred without a judicial order.

I would like to acknowledge former senators Dasko and Omidvar for their work in passing this bill in the Senate. I would also like to thank the very many people who have played a part in getting the bill to where it is today.
Content.ProceduralText: (Motion agreed to and bill read the first time)

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, it is always a pleasure to rise on behalf of the people from Kamloops—Thompson—Nicola.
I have two petitions to present today.

The first is on behalf of 70 signatories from Kamloops—Thompson—Nicola. The signatories exhort the Canadian government to invest in renewable and clean energy. The petitioners also ask for a broad electrical grid and nation building. They again exhort the Canadian government to provide leadership in this area in commitment to the 2030 and 2035 targets.
Mr. Speaker, with the second petition, I rise for, I believe, now the fifth time, to ask for federal funding for the fast-tracking and rebuilding of the iconic Red Bridge in Canada.

The bridge was a landmark that was destroyed by arson. It is something that the people from the Tk'emlúps te Secwépemc area and the people of Kamloops have asked for. Federal funds are needed so the bridge could be rebuilt. Hopefully we will see it in the November 5 budget.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to table five petitions, followed by a sixth. I will quickly read the first one, which has to do with Canada Post. Thousands of people have signed it because they are concerned about the budget cuts and are afraid of losing the services to which they are entitled.
I am therefore tabling these five petitions.
Mr. Speaker, the other petition is, in fact, a response requested by Minister Lightbound to look for new ways to—

I would like to remind everyone in the House that mentioning a minister by name is not permitted. I believe the hon. member was referring to the Minister of Government Transformation, Public Works and Procurement.
Mr. Speaker, that was a quote, but I apologize. I was talking about the minister responsible for Canada Post.
This is the sixth petition I am tabling.
Mr. Speaker, I rise to present two petitions today.

The first one I do not agree with but present in good faith on behalf of my constituents who are concerned about the proposed west coast oil pipeline project. They do not want it built, and I do, but I said that, in good faith, I would present the petition.

Mr. Speaker, the second petition I would like to present today is about the greener homes loan. I am tabling the petition on behalf of residents who are concerned about the affordability of home energy efficiency upgrades, such as heat pumps, and the role those play in reducing greenhouse gas emissions.
The petitioners indicate that the Canada greener homes affordability program has helped thousands of households reduce emissions and improve the energy efficiency of their homes.

The petitioners call upon the Government of Canada to reinstate the program as soon as possible and to provide interest-free financing to help Canadians undertake home retrofits aimed at reducing carbon emissions and home efficiencies.
Mr. Speaker, I am honoured to rise to present e-petition 6929. I mention the number because very close to 28,000 Canadians signed this petition. It is an honour to present it.

The petition deals with really painful disabling diseases that Canadians suffer from in large numbers, yet these particular diseases, despite long diagnostic delays, medical complications and barriers, are not publicly funded and have not been recognized by Health Canada as diseases that are disabling.

The diseases of which I speak, and the petitioners are particularly concerned with, are endometriosis and adenomyosis, which are chronic, painful and disabling yet are not covered in the same way other disabilities are.

The petitioners call on the House of Commons to officially recognize endometriosis and adenomyosis as conditions that qualify as disabilities federally and provincially. The federal government can only really resolve the federal disability program, but it certainly is the case that the Canadian Institutes of Health Research and related agencies play a large role in evidence-based decision making and can help the provinces also recognize this.
Mr. Speaker, it is an honour to table a petition today on behalf of the petitioners.

The petitioners highlight that Canada continues to permit live horses to be exported by air for slaughter for human consumption; that horses are transported from feedlots to Canadian airports and flown overseas in wooden crates, with journeys potentially lasting up to 28 hours without feed, water or rest; that horses are highly sensitive animals with strong fight-or-flight responses, and prolonged transportation and confinement can cause significant stress and expose them to injury, illness and death; that existing federal regulations govern the conditions under which horses may be transported but do not eliminate the inherent welfare concerns associated with long-distance transport for slaughter; and, last, that Canadians have repeatedly called upon Parliament to end this practice through petitions, public advocacy and proposed legislation.

Successive attempts have been made in Parliament to prohibit the live export of horses for slaughter, and the Government of Canada previously committed to ending this practice, yet these exports continue. The petitioners are calling on the government to act without further delay to permanently prohibit the export of live horses from Canada for slaughter for human consumption, including horses exported for fattening before slaughter, through all necessary legislative and regulatory measures.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Kevin Lamoureux (Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I ask that all questions be allowed to stand, please.
Is it agreed?
Some hon. members: Agreed.
[For text of questions and responses, see Written Questions website]
I wish to inform the House that I have received notice of a request for an emergency debate. I invite the hon. member for Lac-Saint-Jean to rise and make a brief intervention.
Mr. Speaker, I am speaking to you today without a shred of cynicism.

I stubbornly refuse to believe that everything governing the functioning of the House is always partisan, and that we can still have essential discussions about the future of Quebec and Canada. If these discussions are urgent, we will recognize their urgency and be willing to discuss them.

As everyone knows, a summit on a new partnership between Canada and Europe was held in Montreal last week, on Thursday and Friday. At the close of the summit, both President of the European Commission Ursula von der Leyen and Canada's Prime Minister stated that Canada will become an associate member of the European Union. It was with that designation that President von der Leyen set off for Europe. Soon, today or tomorrow, European countries will be discussing the status of associate membership.

That is also what the Prime Minister called it at the conclusion of the summit. Meanwhile, how many hours of debate will we have devoted to the status of associate membership? How can Europe discuss the future of Quebec and Canada without the democratically elected men and women of the House having the slightest opportunity to debate it, to share their comments, their position or their concerns? How does the government define “associate membership”? What does this mean for Quebec and the provinces? What are the implications for first nations? What are the implications for the House?

The future of Canada, and therefore of Quebec, may now be unfolding in Strasbourg. The House must debate this matter urgently. I therefore ask that you grant our request and call an emergency debate this evening on this issue.
I thank the hon. member for Lac-Saint-Jean for his remarks, but I do not find that the request meets the requirements of the Standing Orders.

SubjectOfBusinessContent.ParaText: The House resumed consideration of the motion.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Kevin Lamoureux (Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, as I indicated at the outset of my comments, it is always a pleasure to rise and talk about important issues, like our veterans and the way in which governments or arm's-length organizations such as CRA procure and do contracts on a wide spectrum of different things. These are all important issues, and there is no doubt about that. I have a number of things that I would like to say.

First, I would like to make a correction. I might have said that the Canadian Corps of Commissionaires was founded in 2025. It should have been 1925. It was 100 years ago. It actually started in the community of Montreal. The “thirties” I was talking about was obviously the 1930s.

I want to recognize that at the time, there would have been a great deal of discussion about veterans coming home from abroad, whether it was from World War I or World War II. The incredible service provided by the Canadian Corps of Commissionaires was absolutely outstanding, second to likely no other organization. I am not familiar with all the organizations from back then, but I suspect that there would have been a number of non-profits, like the Legion and so forth. There was infrastructure put in place and it was very welcoming. There were many wartime houses being built in our nation in order to accommodate veterans and ensure there was housing for them.

I made reference to the fact that all members of the House, I believe, have an interest in our veterans. This is a very important week. We are all wearing poppies. We wear poppies for a very good reason. It is to recognize past, current and ultimately future serving members and, in dealing with the past, those who made the ultimate sacrifice in regard to their life, among the many other forms of casualties. It is a time at which all Canadians should reflect on the valuable role that members of the Canadian Forces have played for generations.

Having said that, I want to spend some time talking about the issue we have before us. The Conservatives are raising it to try to make it look as if the government is not being sensitive to our veterans. I do not believe that to be the case one iota. In fact, if we look at some of the things we have done since the last election under the leadership of our current Prime Minister and current minister responsible for veterans, I think we see a caring attitude, plus resources.

I can talk about the commitment that was made back in the 2025 budget to enhance veterans' services by improving IT infrastructure. That was an investment of well over $150 million. The purpose of that investment was to ensure that veterans with disabilities who require services are being served in a quicker fashion. The idea was to speed up the process. This was brought forward shortly after the last election.

We had that particular announcement. An announcement also took place last week. The minister labelled it as “veteran-ready”. It is a veteran employer recognition initiative. I believe that type of initiative is going to make a difference and support our veterans in a very real and tangible way.

We need to recognize not only the skill sets that are acquired while serving in the military, but also the education that many members of our forces bring to the military. There are ways we can enhance, amplify, do some fine-tuning or go beyond fine-tuning in order to support our veterans and at the same time recognize our businesses in the community. Not all veterans have PTSD. At the end of the day, there are opportunities for employers to hire outstanding Canadians who have put their lives on the line and have served our country. There is absolutely nothing wrong with promoting that.

In terms of the Commissionaires, I made reference to the late 1920s going into the late 1930s as a time in which life in Canada was very different. We had many veterans, people retiring from the war, from the forces, looking for opportunities. It was a very difficult situation. One can only imagine the horrors of war, whether it was World War I, World War II, the Korean War or what took place in Afghanistan. These are individuals who sacrificed a great deal.

That is why I posed a question in regard to the numbers. The Commissionaires is not quite what it was 30, 40 or 50 years ago. That is not to take anything away from the Commissionaires, but there are not as many veterans for a number of reasons. Veterans do not make up the majority of commissionaires. In fact, I believe it might even be around 20% or just a little higher. Again, that is not to take anything away from the Commissionaires, and I would hope that members would not try to suggest that.

There are many other ways in which we can look at how to support our veterans. I would like to see investments in entrepreneurs, businesses and so forth. There are many companies hiring veterans today, some of them dealing with security.

CRA is the arm's-length, independent corporation responsible for Canadian revenue taxation. At the end of the day, this decision was made based on a number of different factors. However, when we look at the Universal Protection Service, the company that ultimately prevailed on that particular procurement, my understanding is that with the contract, we are talking about 60 individuals across the country. The contract is for 60 positions, if I can put it that way. Out of those, 33 have been rehired. Out of those 33, a dozen are veterans.

I do not want to do a comparison between one company and the other, but I will acknowledge the efforts of the Commissionaires and the role it has played with CRA. I suspect it will be in a good position going into the future to continue to do the fine work it does with veterans.

When I look at the motion we have before us and listen to some of the questions that have been put forward, I question the motivation. Let me give an example from the member who represents the community of Moose Jaw, a beautiful city that I lived in for a couple of years. That is where I had my first job. In many ways, it is a fantastic community.

I would like to quote him because I did write it down and was careful to ensure that I got the actual words he said. The member said, “the Liberal government is going to be unemploying 3,000 veterans”. At the very least, it is misleading. I would like to think that it was not done intentionally, because that would be against the rules of the House. Every member knows and understands that the CRA contract has nothing to do with 3,000 veterans becoming unemployed.

If we look at statements of that nature and then look at the content of the motion before us today, I would pose the question of why the Conservatives have tied in a trip that was made by the Prime Minister and dozens of others to promote Canada and build our economy beyond the Canada-U.S. border. Why did they choose to make reference to that trip and some of the costs? For the Conservatives who were in government in the past, surely to goodness they would recognize that these are not negotiated prices. These prices are set. We are following the same pattern as previous governments. There were a number of people who accompanied. It was a number of different days. There is a certain requirement for security today, for example.

Why did they incorporate that aspect into the motion? In my opinion, it is because they are trying to do two things with it. One is that they are trying to give a false impression that the government does not care about veterans and veterans getting employment after they have been released from the Canadian Forces, which is just not true. The other deals with the issue of something we saw in question period, and that is to try to use character assassination, as opposed to dealing with issues of substance.

I had the chance to ask a couple of questions at the very beginning of the member who introduced the motion and the leader of the Conservative Party. When I asked a question of the member who introduced the motion, I made reference to the latter point that it is very political what the Conservatives are doing. That is the reason they put the flight information down. I used the example of Stephen Harper. The current leader of the Conservative Party was sitting in cabinet when Stephen Harper paid $1 million to fly a car from Canada to India. There are cars in India.
An hon. member: It was for the RCMP, Kevin. You know that.

Hon. Kevin Lamoureux: Mr. Speaker, the member across the way says it was for the RCMP. In one sense, he is starting to make the point. At the end of the day, as I just said, they are trying to assert blame or assert irresponsible spending, and the member opposite just recognized that it would not be fair to say that. The Conservatives have done that and have incorporated it into the motion itself. That is why, from my perspective, it is a politically motivated motion to take shots at the government.

This motion has nothing with regard to our vets, because if it had something to do with vets, where they could get support in a tangible way from the House or challenge the government, there are many ways they could do that. They could challenge the government in what the government, not the CRA, is doing to support our veterans. I would be able to talk about, in detail, the veterans ready initiative, which was just launched last week—
The member will have to find another time to talk about that.
With questions and comments, the hon. member for Saskatoon South has the floor.

Mr. Speaker, with today's opposition motion, we simply want to put Canada first in procurement. We want to honour our veterans. The Corps of Commissionaires in my province of Saskatchewan has been around for decades. I want to salute Lorne Gelowitz, the CEO of northern Saskatchewan, and Dean Rae, the CEO of south Saskatchewan. These are important employment opportunities for Canadians.

In 10 days, Saskatoon will once again host the largest indoor Remembrance Day service in the country. We will have between 7,000 and 10,000 people at 11 o'clock at SaskTel Centre. The Corps of Commissionaires is a vital reason for this.
I just want to say this to the member for Winnipeg North: Let us respect our veterans and reverse this contract.
Mr. Speaker, I do respect veterans. I myself am a veteran. The Prime Minister respects veterans. Every member of the government supports and respects our veterans.

We will attend a multitude of different events that will recognize the many sacrifices made by our veterans in a multitude of different wars, recognizing our veterans, whether they made the ultimate sacrifice or came back with all sorts of health-related issues, in physical health or mental health.

I think it is absolutely critical that we all respect our veterans. I like to think we all do. I myself will go to Brookside, where thousands who lost their lives are laid to rest. I think there are different ways. One of the things is to wear a poppy and support our vets.
Mr. Speaker, the Liberal government has adopted a buy Canadian policy. The Prime Minister has told Canadians that he wants to make Canada its own best customer.

Despite this, the government's actions tell a very different story. Since the Prime Minister took office, six of the 10 largest contracts have been awarded to federal suppliers headquartered in the United States. The Toronto Star reported that the Liberal government has awarded billions of dollars' worth of contracts to American companies. The total now stands at $7.8 billion, according to their data, and the share of contracts going to U.S.-based firms continues to increase.
How does my colleague explain that?
Mr. Speaker, I do not necessarily know the details. The member just brought it forward to the House, at least as far as I have heard.

At the end of the day, I believe that we need to look at the company that received this. It is a subsidiary of an American company. There are many subsidiaries here in Canada with headquarters in the United States, and vice versa. We have headquarters here in Canada where they have subsidiaries in the United States. What is important is the footprint that the subsidiaries have. My understanding is that we are talking about thousands of employees, some of them in Winnipeg.
Mr. Speaker, I want draw on what my colleague on the other side of the House said.
Approximately 4% of government contracts are awarded to U.S. companies. By contrast, a great many contracts are now awarded to Canadian companies.

I would like my colleague to tell me a little about what we are doing with the Davie shipyard, because this will have a significant impact here at home. There is the Davie Shipyard, but there is also the contract for the icebreakers.
I think these are two particularly interesting projects. What is the government's position on these sorts of projects, which are creating jobs here at home?

Mr. Speaker, that was an excellent question. The Davie project is a major project. The province of Quebec and other areas of Canada will benefit from that, much like they will from many other major projects where we see Canadian labour; Canadian steel, lumber, aluminum; and things here in Canada being used to advance those projects.

Canadians themselves are responding. Take a look, for example, at the number of visitors going down to the United States. Take a look at the number of Canadians today who, when they do their shopping, are looking at where that product was manufactured.

Mr. Speaker, first and foremost, Commissionaires is still the largest employer of Canada's veterans, and it is a not-for-profit. The government has been meeting with GardaWorld as recently as July, but Commissionaires cannot even get a meeting with the minister, who has not met with Commissionaires since the spring.

I am hoping my colleague can share a bit of insight on why the government is refusing to meet with the Commissionaires. If there is an issue about needing to increase the amount of veterans who are working for Commissionaires, that should be a conversation the minister is having. Taking that away and giving it to a private company instead is privatization that has crossed the line. It is over the top.
When the member talks about veteran employment, I will tell him what it is like in my riding. In Courtenay, where the Commissionaires is, 60% of those who work for Commissionaires are veterans.
I am hoping my colleague can explain why the minister refuses to meet with Commissionaires.

Mr. Speaker, I have, and I have said this in my comments, an immense amount of respect. I acknowledge the incredible work Commissionaires has done through the years. I believe Commissionaires will continue to be able to provide employment opportunities for veterans. I look to it, as a non-profit organization, to continue to grow. I also recognize there is a genuine attempt by the Commissionaires to employ even a higher percentage of veterans.
When I think of those war veterans from World War II who I marched with, side by side in parades, there are many things they talked about regarding freedoms and the type of—
Questions and comments, the hon. member for Saanich—Gulf Islands.

Mr. Speaker, earlier in his comments, the hon. member for Winnipeg North said something with which I completely agree, and I would like him to underscore the point. I wonder why he did not make the same point to my question of personal privilege, where he disagreed. He said just now, and he is absolutely right, that if there was a misleading statement but no intention to mislead, that was different. It was misinformation, but misinformation with an intent to mislead would violate the rules of this place.

The Speaker is still considering my question of personal privilege, so I ask my hon. friend from Winnipeg North to pitch in here and confirm what he just said, which was correct. “Disinformation” is defined by the Oxford English Dictionary, and any other dictionary, as “deliberately false information” for the purpose of deceit and deception.
Would the hon. member agree that, when an hon. member here accuses other members of deliberate deception by using the word “disinformation”, as he just said, that violates the rules of this place?

Mr. Speaker, I think it is in Beauchesne's sixth edition where it talks about the Speaker's ability to use discretion as there is not any given word that is parliamentary or unparliamentary. Often, it is the context in which someone says something. For example, I can say, “It is absolutely misleading when members stand up in this chamber to say something that is just not true.” I would be very careful in terms of using the word “lie,” but I could say that. However, if I were to attribute it to an individual specifically, there is a chance the member might stand up on a point of order and ask me to apologize.
I think it is not quite as simple as the member opposite says. I am sympathetic to what she is saying, but I do not believe that—
Questions and comments, the hon. member for Laurentides—Labelle.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to know why the government is creating so many new agencies and why, every time we ask about the reasons for a decision, we are told that it was not a government decision. The procurement ombud has said that this has got to stop.

Is the government, which keeps creating new agencies, prepared to give the procurement ombud the authority to oversee their procurement activities in the same way that he oversees other government contracts?

Mr. Speaker, I am not 100% sure that I understand the question. I do believe it is important that the government has set up corporations and agencies, and there is great value to that. We have seen provinces use them as arm's-length organizations. There are procurement processes and procedures often recommended by governments, no matter what level they might be, and there is a sense of accountability to that. I would like to think that the CRA, which is independent and arm's-length from government, is making the decision based on the criteria it established and set out when it put it out for tender.
Mr. Speaker, I will be sharing my time with my colleague from Airdrie—Cochrane.
“Sensitivity” is a word that I would like members to remember because I am going to come back to it in my speech.

I want to talk about the word “sensitivity” because, in a few days, Canadians will gather for Remembrance Day ceremonies. They will wear a poppy, just as we are all doing right now here in the House. In each of our regions, we will honour our veterans and soldiers who have been deployed to various missions abroad. We will also thank their families for the sacrifices they have made throughout Canada's history in times of war by entrusting a member of their family to the service of our country in order to protect Canada and the freedoms that we now enjoy.

The people who devoted years to serving our country are the reason for these ceremonies. Some of them have been deployed far from their loved ones. Others are still living with injuries sustained while on duty. When they leave the armed forces, these people need to continue to earn a living and take care of their families. That is something that the public is not often aware of. A soldier is not always a soldier. A person does not remain a soldier their whole life, except maybe in their heart. They have to make a living and get back into the swing of everyday life. That is exactly what many members of the Canadian Armed Forces have to do.
