Content.ParaText: It was interesting hearing the member opposite talk about fool's gold. I guess he is an expert in that, especially in conspiracy theories.

We are doing this study right now in the government operations and estimates committee, and the definition of what is Canadian has been explained to the member, I do even know how many times. It is a physical presence in Canada, tax registration and sourcing of Canadian goods and labour. It is pretty straightforward. It also follows well-established practices.
Would the member opposite agree that Canada's buy Canadian policy is important in the context of a global trade war?

Mr. Speaker, I cannot believe the member actually just stated that. He is telling me that the government actually supports dealing the buy Canadian policy to companies such as Huawei. It simply has corporate affairs in here. It has been registered and identified as a national threat to our country, and it is okay for our government to be buying products from Huawei. Is that what the member is telling me?

Mr. Speaker, we in the Bloc Québécois agree with the part of the motion that deals with the buy Canadian policy. However, there is another part that runs counter to secularism or that supports the use of religious language by chaplains. There is also a part that mentions steel, aluminum and lumber in the preamble, but the motion does not address them further.
What exactly is the overall message of this motion?

Mr. Speaker, the global message from the Liberal government is that it values veterans less than it values American companies, which is absolutely shameful and disgusting. I cannot imagine being a veteran here, going to defend our country and then coming back to a slap in the face. It is absolutely deplorable.

Mr. Speaker, there are two issues we are talking about. One is an American company's getting a contract that is normally reserved for the veterans of Canada, those who served in our armed forces. However, more importantly, the non-profit Commissionaires uses the revenue to help veterans from the armed forces who otherwise would not have it. The company in question, Allied Universal, a United States-based company, is not going to provide that same service to our veterans. Can the member please comment on that?

Mr. Speaker, the member asked a very good question. What kind of government that is supposed to be looking after our country and our veterans would consider that to be a good, very sound decision and as standing up for Canada? I can tell the House that a Conservative government would never make that kind of decision.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Kevin Lamoureux (Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, gross exaggeration is probably one of the ways I would describe many of the comments made by my friend across the way. The company he is shooting down employs Manitobans. The footprint in Canada is significantly large. The Commissionaires defend the commissionaires until the end. At the end of the day, I believe in the support they give.

However, the member should not give the false impression that the commissionaires are 100% veterans. They are not. It is probably closer to about 20%, and the company that has taken over the contract has rehired 30, maybe 33, of the 60 who were working there, a dozen of whom are veterans. Let us not grossly exaggerate the situation. Would the member not agree?
Mr. Speaker, the member said “false impression”. My gosh, it is smoke and mirrors. The Liberals are masters at this. They are absolutely outraged. How dare we question one thing about this policy?
I went on for 10 minutes explaining to the Canadian public and to all those attending here today how much the government is misleading Canadians. It has to stop.
The bigger question is, what kind of government would do this to the Canadian people?
Mr. Speaker, I would like to start by saying I will be sharing my time with the member for Surrey Newton.

I welcome the opportunity to debate the motion from the hon. member for Battle River—Crowfoot. At a time of open challenges to our economic security and sovereignty, I can think of few more pressing public policy issues than the question of where and when key government contracts go to Canadian firms and suppliers. This is at the root of the motion put to us today, and I can assure all members that the government shares this concern.

Since last December, the buy Canadian policy has been at the centre of a suite of measures introduced by the Government of Canada to stimulate the growth of Canada's builders and suppliers. Last September, we launched Build Canada Homes, a new federal agency that is building affordable housing at scale, fuelling a new and thriving housing industry. With an initial investment of $13 billion over five years, Build Canada Homes is investing in the development of public lands sites in partnership with Canadian builders, suppliers, other levels of government and indigenous communities. That investment is already making a difference, with multiple direct-build projects across multiple cities delivering up to 4,000 new homes on federal land, with at least 40% at below market rents.

There is also the Defence Investment Agency. The need for a more strategic and responsive approach to defence procurement has long been acknowledged in Canada, but only in the last year has real action been taken. Since its inception last October, the Defence Investment Agency has been delivering for the Canadian Armed Forces while driving investment, innovation and industrial growth by targeting procurements that support strategic defence sectors such as aerospace and advanced manufacturing. The agency is driving the creation of high-quality, skilled jobs to communities across Canada and bolstering our country's industrial capacity and technological competitiveness.

Finally, the Major Projects Office was introduced last year to put transformative, nation-building ideas on a viable path to fruition through the co-operation of federal departments, provinces and territories, indigenous peoples and industry. The goal is to identify projects with maximum benefit for Canadians. For example, just last month, the government announced that the new west coast pipeline, known as Pacific link, would be listed as a project of national interest.

Whether it is the need for affordable housing, state-of-the-art defence capabilities or major infrastructure, these initiatives do not simply recognize the great reservoir of talent and experience within Canadian industry. They bank on it, and so does the buy Canadian policy. In fact, the policy is something of a common thread that runs through all these initiatives. The buy Canadian policy prioritizes Canadian suppliers and materials, strengthens supply chains and incentivizes Canadian content in strategic federal procurements. It applies to the ongoing work of the Major Projects Office, the Defence Investment Agency, Build Canada Homes and Crown corporations and their subsidies, as well as the hundreds of federal grants and contributions programs.

In just over eight months, between December and October, Public Services and Procurement Canada awarded over 1,600 new contracts, worth approximately $23.8 billion. Of these, roughly 1,340 contracts totalling $17.7 billion were awarded to suppliers operating in Canada. These efforts are transforming local communities across the country with long-term, well-paying job opportunities for skilled workers.

Last February, Kitchener's Colt Canada was awarded a $307-million contract to supply the Canadian Armed Forces with assault rifle systems under the Canadian modular assault rifle project. By investing in local expertise, we are ensuring that the forces are ready for the challenges ahead.

In August, the government awarded a $768.6-million construction services contract to PCL Constructors Canada for the full construction of a new federal regulatory science facility at the Canadian Food Inspection Agency's Ottawa laboratory in Nepean, Ontario. On average, the site will employ about 250 workers a day.

Also last summer, the government announced an investment of $2 billion over four years to General Dynamics Land Systems-Canada to build 190 armoured combat support vehicles. This strategic partnership is truly a pan-Canadian feat of co-operation, with several companies supporting the effort.

Ryan Manufacturing in Richmond, BC, will supply military-grade cable and wire harness assemblies. InterPro in Regina, Saskatchewan, will supply advanced armour. Thales Canada in Saint-Laurent, Quebec, will supply thermal imaging systems. IMP Aerospace and Defence in Enfield, Nova Scotia, will supply other specialized components. The difference under the buy Canadian policy is that Canadian suppliers are now prioritized as a matter of practice. Suppliers must demonstrate that they meet the policy requirements, including through eligibility and Canadian content attestations, and the government has put compliance and monitoring mechanisms in place.

The buy Canadian policy goes beyond giving preference to Canadian suppliers. In strategic federal procurements covered by the policy, bids receive additional evaluation points for higher proportions of Canadian content and value added activities, such as manufacturing and research development. This encourages businesses to source more from Canadian partners, extending opportunities to Canadian firms that supply components, materials and expertise. Our goal is to create an incentive for businesses to do more in Canada and to have more Canadian workers, more Canadian suppliers in their supply chains, more Canadian manufacturing, more Canadian research and development, and more investment in Canadian facilities and communities.

In conclusion, it was said once that the world needs more Canada. With these policies and programs, the government is taking the position that Canada needs more Canada. International co-operation with trusted partners, both public and private, will always be a part of our efforts as a responsible federal government, but if the last two years have taught us anything, it is that our future is best placed in our own hands. We have made significant progress in less than a year, but this is not the finish line. We will continue expanding opportunities for Canadian businesses, strengthening Canadian supply chains and ensuring that federal government procurement serves as an economic lever for this country, because federal procurement is more than just purchases; it is an opportunity to build Canadian capacity, support Canadian workers and invest in Canada's economic future.
This is the essence of the buy Canadian policy, and I look forward to seeing where it takes us in the years ahead.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank the member from Winnipeg for outlining, in general terms, the buy Canada policy. In reality, many small businesses across our country do not know where to start or where to go to apply for a government contract. In addition to that, the red tape to enter into an agreement is still very challenging for many of the small businesses that are facing the uncertainty referenced in his speech.

In good faith, what areas can the government improve in procurement to actually see small businesses take up the government contracts? Since the announcements from the secretary of state for small business have come into force, we have not seen the increase in those contracts going to Canadian firms.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member's question is a very good question. It is a very timely question. We do know that, when a new program is introduced, there are questions. We need to be expanding what we are doing and the information we make available, but the offices of members of Parliament are already available. My own office, and I am sure the hon. member's office as well, is assisting small businesses in the riding to take advantage of these important government programs.

Mr. Speaker, I listened carefully to my colleague's speech. He is well aware that the government has a long-standing relationship with this organization, whose social mission is to help our veterans transition to civilian life is. The response we are hearing is that this decision was a matter of efficiency, taken in response to the current context, and that few thousand people is minor. The government upended an arrangement that had existed for over a hundred years.
How does my colleague think a veteran would react to hearing that?
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate my colleague's valuable work with me on the health committee.

Yes, we do have a social contract with our veterans, and there are established practices, but of course we talk about things that have been going on for over 100 years. A hundred years is a long time. There are going to be changes in our processes. Our government procurement decisions have to be made with the best decisions for all stakeholders in Canada at the time.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to follow up on a question from the opposition regarding the claim that the government does not support small businesses and that they do not have access to federal contracts.

I believe that the small business procurement program, which was introduced over the summer, helps by simplifying procurement processes, scaling contracts for SMEs and supporting small businesses in gaining access to contracting opportunities.
I would like to ask my colleague whether he himself takes steps in his riding to assist businesses seeking to obtain contracts with the federal government.
If so, what exactly is he doing?

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member is absolutely right. The process is being streamlined. I, like I am sure almost every MP in here, have people working in my office who work directly with constituents, including constituent companies. When they call us, they want to know what is available. We make sure that they know the programs that are available and exactly how the process works. If they have problems with the process, we can help them navigate those and call the relevant departments for clarification.

Mr. Speaker, I rise in the House today to reaffirm the Government of Canada's commitment to the buy Canadian policy. We are incredibly proud of how this initiative is transforming government procurement, giving Canadian businesses, workers, manufacturers and suppliers greater access to opportunities and delivering real results for Canada.

The government will always stand with Canadian workers and Canadian businesses, and that is how we will build the strongest economy in the G7. We remain committed to prioritizing Canadian suppliers and Canadian-made goods and services in federal procurement.

This is a pledge we have made to Canadians and it is unwavering. Since the buy Canadian policy came into force in December 2025, it has been reshaping how the federal government spends by prioritizing Canadian content, materials, suppliers and workers at every opportunity. From steel and aluminum to wood products, the government's purchasing of goods and services is being used as a powerful tool to back key industries and strengthen domestic supply chains.

The rollout of the buy Canadian policy marked a major step toward building a more resilient Canadian economy. It was designed to ensure clear advantages are available to suppliers who invest, innovate and produce here at home. By prioritizing Canadian suppliers, Canadian materials and Canadian content in federal procurement, we are becoming our own best customer by reducing reliance on any single trading partner and building—
I have to interrupt the member.
The member for Laurentides—Labelle is rising on a point of order.
Mr. Speaker, I am very sorry to have to interrupt my colleague, but the interpretation has stopped. It is important for me to be able to understand what he is saying.
I believe the member has a mobile device, perhaps either in his pocket or on the table, that is interfering with interpretation. I will ask him to put it away or put it on airplane mode.
The member can restart, and we can give him back about 20 seconds' worth of time so that interpretation can work again. I will ask him to keep the mobile device away from the speakers.

Mr. Speaker, by prioritizing Canadian suppliers, Canadian materials and Canadian content in federal procurement, we are becoming our own best customer. By reducing our reliance on any single trading partner and building resilience through strong domestic demand, we are bolstering Canada's economy. The policy on prioritizing Canadian suppliers and Canadian content in strategic federal procurements initially applied to procurements valued at $25 million or more. In June, we lowered that threshold to $5 million, significantly expanding its reach.

We are also putting Canadian materials at the centre of major federal construction and defence projects. For procurement of $25 million or more, the policy requires Canadian-produced steel, aluminum and wood. We are making it easier for Canadian small businesses to compete for federal opportunities through the small business procurement program, which will simplify procurement processes and introduce new digital tools.

Ultimately, the test of this policy is whether federal spending creates economic activity here at home. In the spirit of the buy Canadian policy, the government continues to work to identify opportunities for Canadian suppliers to benefit from federal procurement policies and ultimately support Canadian workers, Canadian businesses and Canadian communities. This includes attracting investments that deliver tangible and lasting benefits to Canadian communities and supply chains.

This is about driving growth, creating opportunities and enhancing prosperity for all Canadians. In the current situation we are in, this has never been more important, particularly when it comes to protecting Canada's sovereignty. We know that the world has changed and that Canada must change with it. That is why Canada is also making generational investments to rebuild and reinvest in the Canadian Armed Forces. These investments are guided by Canada's first-ever defence industrial strategy, a whole-of-government approach to transform Canada's defence industry. The strategy will prioritize Canadian suppliers and materials, invest in Canadian innovation and streamline defence procurement. It is supported by the new Defence Investment Agency.

Between December 2025 and October 1, 2026, Public Services and Procurement Canada awarded a total of 1,644 new contracts worth roughly $23 billion. Of these, 1,342 contracts, representing about $17.7 billion, were awarded to suppliers operating here in Canada. That is the kind of progress we want to build on.

With regard to today's motion, the Canada Revenue Agency, following a fair and open procurement process, decided to award the contract to a company that operates extensively in Canada and employs Canadian security guards, supervisors and managers. This brings me to an important point of what we mean when we talk about a Canadian supplier.

Being a Canadian supplier is not simply a question of who owns the shares of a company. We also need to look at where the economic activity takes place. Under the buy Canadian policy, the definition of Canadian supplier is based on substantive economic activity in Canada. That includes having a place of business here, being registered here, filing taxes here, conducting ongoing activities and employing people in Canada to deliver goods and services. That distinction matters.

A company can be part of a global enterprise and still employ thousands of Canadians. It can pay taxes here. It can operate facilities here. It can conduct research and development here, and it can purchase from Canadian suppliers and invest in Canadian communities. Those jobs are Canadian jobs. Those investments are investments in Canada, and that economic activity matters to Canadians and Canada.

Buy Canadian is not simply about where a company's headquarters is located. It is about where the jobs are, where the investment is, where the innovation happens, where the supply chain is built and ultimately, where the economic benefits land. We continue to work closely with businesses, suppliers and stakeholders to develop and refine procurement measures that support Canadian industry, strengthen supply chains and drive our country's economic growth.
Our government will always stand with Canadian workers and Canadian businesses, and we will build a stronger economy in the G7. We will always support our veterans with job opportunities.

I want to assure this House that we are fully committed to our buy Canadian policy, the substantial opportunities it is providing for Canadians and the powerful benefits for our country. We are transforming our economy through buy Canadian. We are supporting our industries today while keeping a clear focus on this sustainable future. That is our promise to Canadians, which is one that we are delivering on.

Mr. Speaker, the member outlined, in reference to some of the criticisms of the program, namely, the change of threshold from $25 million down to $5 million, but there are still certain policies related to the buy Canada policy at large that need to be addressed, largely related to subcontracting. Some have labelled it a superficial economic illusion that dilutes the intended benefits of this policy we all support.

Is the government open to changing some of the subcontracting policies to allow for that work to stay in Canada and not be sent offshore to non-Canadian entities when the policy in and of itself is to support Canadian small businesses and Canadian companies?

Mr. Speaker, the member understands very well that I come from a small business, and 85% of the businesses in my constituency, in fact even in his constituency, are small businesses. That is where our government's focus is: lowering that threshold from $25 million to $5 million, and now we are looking at other ways the government can provide support.

He and I have to keep advocating and making sure that our government does what is necessary for small businesses to succeed. That is what I will continue to fight for, and that is what I have been fighting for in the many years I have been in Parliament.

Mr. Speaker, since the Prime Minister took office, six of the top 10 federal suppliers are headquartered in the United States. It has been reported that billions of dollars in contracts are still going to American companies, contracts worth a total of $7.8 billion, according to the Toronto Star. It has been reported that the percentage of contracts awarded to American companies is increasing. IBM was cited as an example of buying Canadian earlier because that company has a subsidiary in the member's riding.
How are these contracts divvied up? In my colleague's opinion, what criteria should be used to ensure the government actually does buy Canadian?

Mr. Speaker, as I mentioned earlier, most of these projects have gone to Canadian companies. If we look at the numbers I talked about, between December 2025 and October 1, 2026, Public Services and Procurement Canada awarded a total of 1,644 contracts worth roughly $23 billion. Of these, 1,342 contracts, representing about $17.7 billion, were awarded to suppliers operating in Canada. That is the kind of progress we want to build on, and we will continue to build on having more contracts going to Canadian suppliers in the coming days, weeks, months and years.

Mr. Speaker, when I first came to the House in 2015, I remember that the defence budget was less than 1% of GDP. Now it is over 2%. Of course, the economy has also grown in that perspective, which means it is actually a tripling of the defence budget. We have similarly seen increases in the Veterans Affairs budget. I think everyone in the House agrees we need to build Canada strong, we need to hire more Canadians and we need to buy more in Canada.
Would my friend, like to comment on the significant investments and the improvements we have made both for Canadian defence and for Canadian veterans?

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member has already answered the question that he asked. There was a promise made by our government and a promise kept when it comes to veterans and making sure that we take good care of veterans. Every member of the House, irrespective of the side of the House they are on, respects the sacrifices they made, and we will continue to work hard for those veterans and—
Resuming debate, the hon. member for Vernon—Lake Country—Monashee.
Mr. Speaker, I will be sharing my time with the member for Cowichan—Malahat—Langford.

There is an increasingly familiar pattern emerging from the Liberals. The Prime Minister of this 11-year-old government makes grand new announcements about Canadian sovereignty, and Canadians are assured that a bold new era of government is about to arrive. Unfortunately for the government, somebody always pulls back the curtain to see what is behind it, and that is where the troubles start.

This truly is a government of loud announcements and empty promises. For example, the Liberals backslapped each other over reaching our nation's 2% NATO commitment. Only later did we discover that it includes an unarmed, unionized civilian Coast Guard. Projects like the F-35 are stalling amid political games. The PBO cannot provide a clear picture of what the future holds, and, increasingly, it looks like the Liberals cannot either.

There is a difference between grandstanding and governing. Grandstanding is convincing Canadians that they believe in something. Governing involves showing them when decisions actually have to be made. The Prime Minister seems more interested in Brussels and Middle Eastern controversies than Canadian veterans.

We are talking about the Canadian Corps of Commissionaires, an institution that has served veterans for a century. I served as a captain in the Canadian Army Reserve, and that experience gave me an appreciation for the military that goes well beyond government documents. One thing people learn in university is the ethics of duty. They also learn that the military does not disappear from our lives the minute we take off the uniform.

My father passed away many years ago, but I want to revive an argument we had when he was alive. I think, looking back, he would be okay with that. My dad was a young air force officer who later scoffed at veterans attending military functions in uniform after retiring. He said that they were living in the past. He called them old soldiers who kept reliving their glory days. I heard my dad then. I disagree with him now.

I think veterans carry what they have learned in the military forward in life, regardless of whether they retire after one tour or after most of their working lives. Here is what my father learned, and I do not think he would mind me sharing it. He was a farm boy who joined the air force to become a pilot, because pilots were cool. That is pretty much the only reason. Here is what happened. He failed. He became a bombardier instead. He completed one tour of duty, and then he largely avoided military events afterward.

However, he learned something in the military. He learned that he did not like failure. In fact, he apparently made the grandiose promise to my mother that he would never fail again. Now, I do not know what my dad's win-loss column was in life, and I do not think it matters that much, but he learned a lesson, admitted it and moved on. He went on to earn a Ph.D., become an internationally famous biologist and later in life received the university gold medal as the most accomplished graduate of his undergraduate class. I suspect that hard work brought him more success than failure.

Other veterans take different paths, and many of them stay in longer and need help making the transition to civilian life. That is why we need organizations like the Commissionaires. The Canadian Corps of Commissionaires was created in 1925 to help returning soldiers with employment. Today it employs about 22,000 Canadians, including thousands of veterans. It is a Canadian not-for-profit organization, and it is our country's largest employer of veterans. It recognizes military experience, and it offers veterans a way to keep contributing.

One would think that an organization like that would pretty well fit into the Prime Minister's buy Canadian economic sovereignty plan. Of course there is this enthusiasm for telling the rest of us to buy Canadian. In response to President Trump's trade war, he first promised a deal. When that failed, he promised federal spending would default to Canadian suppliers. When his buy Canada policy took effect in December 2025, he declared that Canada would become its own best customer.

Unfortunately, when it came to an actual procurement decision, the Canadian content of his political record turned out to be greater than his appreciation of Canadian ownership. Let us look at the CRA contract. In June, the Canada Revenue Agency awarded a contract worth nearly $12 million, not to the Commissionaires, a Canadian non-profit dedicated to helping veterans. Nope. It was awarded to UPSSC, a Canadian subsidiary of an American multinational, Allied Universal.

The difference between the bids was about $80,000, which is less than the cost of the Prime Minister's banquet bill. It is a 1% difference between a Canadian veteran organization and an American multinational. So much for buy Canadian. So much for Liberal promises.

Obviously, governments have to get value for taxpayers' money, and I am not arguing that the Commissionaires should automatically win every contract by virtue of just being Canadian, but the government should be able to tell us why it did not value Canadian ownership and veteran employment more than the cost of a prime ministerial banquet. If the assessment was fair, it should release the criteria and explain the decision to Canadians.

The $80,000 gets interesting when we examine government spending priorities. According to a government response to an Order Paper question, catering aboard an aircraft carrying the Prime Minister and his entourage during one trip to China, Qatar and Davos cost well over $100,000. I am not suggesting the Prime Minister should go hungry abroad, but apparently there is considerable flexibility when it comes to expenditures at 35,000 feet.

Apparently, veterans ask too much of the government. The government explanation is that Allied Universal operates through a Canadian subsidiary. I have no criticism of its Canadian workers, but that is not really the point. If an American-owned multinational with a Canadian address is the same thing as a Canadian not-for-profit dedicated to veterans, what exactly does buy Canadian mean?

There is nothing wrong with hiring American companies, but this is a Prime Minister who has made anger at Donald Trump central to his government, and his government awarded a federal contract to an American-owned company with substantial business ties to the Trump administration. Apparently, his elbows are up for the camera but down when the contracts are signed.

What is buy Canadian supposed to mean? If we treat Canadian not-for-profits no differently from foreign-owned companies, ministers should say so. They should also explain to Canadians why they say one thing and do another. Maybe the procurement process did follow the rules, but if those rules do not recognize the value of Canadian veteran employment in a period the Prime Minister himself calls Canada first, then it is the rules that need changing.

We should demand a remedy, not another excuse. Quite honestly, what is the message that Canadians are supposed to get from this fiasco? The Prime Minister wants to sell Canadians on buy European. His ministers want to sell us on buy Canadian, and the groaning bureaucracy of procurement buys American.

I will finish with what my father taught me. He wanted to be a pilot and failed, but he did not spend his life redefining success or explaining away that disappointment. He accepted it, learned from it and went on to accomplish extraordinary things. I still disagreed with him about those “old soldiers”, but he was absolutely right about failure.

As Remembrance Day approaches, ministers will again solemnly tell Canadians how much they respect our veterans, but respect is demonstrated through deeds, not speeches. The government should begin by admitting that passing over a centuries-old veterans institution while campaigning on buy Canadian is at least a decision worth revisiting.

My father understood that failure was not something to disguise with an excuse. It was something to learn from. What matters is what we do afterward. He learned from failure and went on to an extraordinary life. The Prime Minister still has that opportunity with the government, but first, he will have to do something that seems remarkably difficult for the government: He will have to admit that he made a mistake.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Kevin Lamoureux (Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, throughout the day, the member has heard different types of arguments that provide the answers to many of the questions he posed, but of course, the Conservatives do not want to listen to the answers. Rather, they have their spin and speaking lines to try to give a gross exaggeration of the reality of this.

For example, the company that won the award has thousands of employees, some of them in my own province of Manitoba. It has a very significant footprint. CRA is independent of the government in putting out tenders. The Commissionaires, which is a fantastic organization that I have been saying nothing but positive things about, has evolved.
Does the member know what percentage of the Commissionaires is made up of veterans?
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the Liberal logic that goes into this.

Let me talk about the F-35 for a minute. It is from an American-owned company. It would create between 2,500 and 5,000 Canadian jobs and thousands of indirect jobs, and it just happens to be the only airplane that could provide deterrence in the Arctic. By that logic, we should pick the F-35, yet we cannot do that. We will not do that. For some reason, we are just going to wait for a while.
If Canadian jobs and American ownership are not an issue, why do we not have the F-35?

Mr. Speaker, it is clear that there is a rather blurred line between buying Canadian and buying from American subsidiaries. Earlier, a member gave IBM as an example of buying Canadian because IBM has had a subsidiary in her riding for a long time.
What criteria does my colleague think should be used to determine whether a business is Canadian, as opposed to an American business with subsidiaries in Canada?

Mr. Speaker, my job is not to determine the exact makeup, but I will say that when we have something as glaring as an American-owned company and a Canadian-owned non-profit, we do not need to take it to a large jury to find out which one we should be picking.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to recognize my colleague's service and his father's service. It was very nicely woven into his speech today.

He was just speaking about the not-for-profit organization, where money is reinvested into veterans. I would like to hear his thoughts on that as an excuse. Why would the Liberals not want to keep a contract with the Commissionaires, which does such great work and supports veterans?

Mr. Speaker, I think it is fairly obvious that we should be, and it is unfortunate that the Liberals refuse to admit the mistake. It is a simple mistake. They should just change it. Let us buy Canadian again if we are going to buy Canadian.

Unfortunately, with the Liberals, the logic seems to shift a lot. It shifts one way for the F-35, but if we are talking about something else, it will shift another way. We have competing logics that run around, and whatever applies at any given time is the logic they are using.
Mr. Speaker, I have good news. We do have the F-35s. We have Canadian pilots being trained on the F-35s. Would the member acknowledge and express his appreciation for the fact that we have them?
Mr. Speaker, 88 have been scheduled, but we do not have 88, nor do we have a go-ahead on those 88.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today in support of our motion on federal procurement. I rise to speak about our flag and the Canadians who fought under it. I rise for the veterans of Cowichan—Malahat—Langford on Vancouver Island. I rise for the commissionaires who stand watch at our federal buildings. I rise for all the families who have been handed a folded flag.

I served under that flag for 28 years. I have conducted many burials at sea, and I have handed that flag to grieving families, including a father and his two sons. I know the cost those who serve under that flag pay.

The motion before us may be about one contract, but veterans will tell us it is about much more than just one contract. It is about a pattern of betrayal. We can consider that just this year, with respect to Bill C-11, the government waited until the last minute to reverse amendments agreed upon in committee and ignored the survivors of military sexual trauma. They told me it felt like the government had spat in their faces. We can consider new restrictions on military clergy of every faith, even on Remembrance Day; or veterans poisoned by mefloquine in Somalia, fighting their own government in court for over 25 years; or veterans who asked for help and were instead offered euthanasia by Veterans Affairs Canada.
Now let us consider the Commissionaires.

I will remind the Liberal members opposite, who seem to have forgotten, who the commissionaires are. In 1915, in the middle of the First World War, the governor-general proposed a corps to give returning soldiers meaningful work. In 1925, the Canadian Corps of Commissionaires was founded with one commitment. Those who served Canada would come home and not be forgotten. For more than 100 years, that commitment had been kept. For generations, Ottawa stood behind it with a right of first refusal. Before a federal government department's security contract was opened to bidding, it was first offered to the Commissionaires, yet in February, with a single stroke of a pen, the Minister of Veterans Affairs ended that right. Though veterans affairs officials said the department wanted to reassess the right of first refusal, it simply cancelled it.

Then came this contract. The CRA posted it as open only to Canadian suppliers. Here is what most Canadians do not know. Under the current government's new buy Canadian rules, a supplier needs only a place of business in Canada. No one asks who owns the company or where its headquarters are. That is how the Canadian subsidiary of Allied Universal, an American company, qualified. By the company's own numbers, just 1.3% of its 700,000-strong workforce is in Canada. It won the CRA contract by undercutting the Commissionaires by less than 1% of the contract value, or only $80,000.

Now let us hold the government to its own words. Again and again, the Prime Minister has promised that Canada would become our own best customer. He said, “we will select Canadian suppliers by default.” In January, he told Canadians yet again, “We'll buy Canadian. We'll build Canadian.” Well, the CRA had a Canadian supplier, a not-for-profit built for veterans, and when the moment came to be our own best customer, the government went shopping in America.

The Secretary of State for the Canada Revenue Agency says politicians are never involved in the CRA's decisions, and that is true of the contract scoring but not true of the rules. The CRA runs the competition, but the government writes the rules for the CRA to follow, and the government chose a buy Canadian policy with no test of ownership. Those were not the CRA's choices. They were the government's choices.

Last November, the Prime Minister declared that Canadians must honour our veterans' patriotism with our own, and for once, I agree with his words, but his actions ring hollow. Patriotism is not a line in a statement. In this case, it is a choice in that contract.

The government also defends this decision by claiming the Commissionaires could no longer meet its veteran hiring target. Here is what the government will not tell us. The Commissionaires knew the target was a problem. The organization raised it itself. It asked veterans affairs to reassess the target and to update it. Instead, the door was closed. The Commissionaires, which is a not-for-profit, reportedly could not get a meeting with the minister. Meanwhile, senior officials found time to quietly meet with for-profit competitors. Lobbying records prove this.

Allied Universal has had a registered lobbyist working the Canadian government since at least 2023, pursuing federal security contracts exactly like this one, yet only three years ago, the department's own briefing said that the right of first refusal was still aligned with the Government of Canada's priorities. What changed? It is not the veterans but the government. The government called it a competitive procurement process, but this is not competition. This is a retreat.

Here is the kicker. Allied Universal's Canadian subsidiary is suing the Government of Canada for $420 million. It lost a federal airport screening contract and took the government to court. Let us consider what the Liberals have done. In a courtroom, Allied is fighting the government. Meanwhile, in an office, the government is handing an American company a contract taken from our commissionaires, who should be protected by the right of refusal that is not set to expire until next year.

Let us look at Allied Universal's work with the Trump administration. According to public reporting, it has received more than $290 million U.S. from the Department of Homeland Security this year alone, and its subsidiary received $83 million U.S. from ICE, the agency running the Trump deportation program. This summer, Newsweek named Allied Universal one of America's most patriotic companies, and I do not doubt that it is. It is an American company, and it should be proud of that honour. However, I would ask the members opposite this: Since when is it the Canadian government's job to reward America's most patriotic companies? Canada already has its own patriotic organization, and has had for more than 100 years, called the Commissionaires.

Eighteen months ago, the Prime Minister asked Canadians to trust him to stand up to Washington, and many Canadians gave him their trust and their vote for the first time in their life. They believed he was the only one who could handle the president and get a deal. They did not vote to send the veterans contract to a company tied to an American deportation program.

Every Canadian who trusted the Liberal slogans should know this: They did not misplace their patriotism. The government misplaced their trust. At election time, the Liberals wrapped themselves in the flag, but at contract time, they pay Americans. At election time, they stand at the cenotaph, but at contract time, they leave the commissionaires standing at the door. At election time, the government promises to put Canada first, but at contract time, it puts Canada second. I can assure the members opposite that veterans from Vancouver Island to Newfoundland are watching the government closely.
It is not enough to expose the illusion, so let me set out plainly how a government that keeps its word to veterans would restore that promise.

First, it would give the CRA contract back to the commissionaires. Second, it would have Veterans Affairs restore the right of first refusal and update the promise made generations ago to reflect the veterans of today. According to court filings in 2025, the department's own deputy minister suggested renewing that policy with new measures strengthening our commissionaires, not cutting them down. Third, it would lift the restrictions on clergy, the priests, imams, rabbis and other faith leaders, who serve in uniform, so they may pray in their own faith at public ceremonies, Remembrance Day included. Fourth, it would stop fighting veterans in court, sit down with them, hear them and come to an agreement.

Let us end where we began, with the flag I handed to the father and his sons. Veterans define what it means to be Canadian. They come from every province and territory and every faith background and walk of life. From Vimy to Juno Beach to Kandahar, our veterans raised their hand and swore to our flag. They never asked what the flag would give them. They asked what it needed.

I am proud to have served. I am proud to be Canadian. I say to the government and to every member opposite plainly, be Canadian. Be Canadian when the cameras are gone and the contract is signed. Be Canadian in the courtroom, at the cenotaph and at the chapel. Be Canadian for veterans who put Canada first. Keep your promises, honour your own words, and if you cannot be Canadian, then for the love of this country, step aside for those who will. Our flag is not a costume for election time. It is a sacred promise. Our soldiers fought and died for it, and our veterans kept that promise. It is time the government did the same.

Mr. Speaker, the fact that the Liberal government has not only taken jobs away from veterans but has decided to give them to a company that is involved with ICE in the United States is absolutely appalling.

There are a lot of veterans living in Winnipeg Centre who are houseless and do not have a livable income. I have talked to many veterans organizations in Winnipeg that support my idea of a guaranteed livable basic income. Veterans make a sacrifice for whatever reasons they find in their spirit, but when they come back, we do not look after them. It is not only through employment but also if they are unable to work for whatever reason.
I am wondering if the member supports my idea of putting in place a guaranteed livable basic income for veterans.

Mr. Speaker, the homelessness of veterans is a horrible crisis this country faces. In fact, I was just at a home for veterans in Ottawa serving Thanksgiving dinner to them not too long ago. If the government was running the economy the way it pretends it does and was giving and protecting veterans' jobs, that would not be necessary. Our veterans would have jobs, would be working for the Commissionaires and would not be homeless.
Mr. Speaker, I cannot help but share his dismay as we watch the government create more and more agencies and Crown corporations. We can certainly add the Allied Universal contract to that list.
This removes accountability from the minister. It reduces transparency. It takes democratic power away from this House.
I would like to hear my colleague's views on this trend. Is he as concerned about this as I am?

Mr. Speaker, indeed, a common trend is not just betraying veterans, as I outlined in my speech, but a lack of accountability. We see that with the Defence Investment Agency. Absolutely, I am outraged at some of the accountability issues, the irresponsible spending and the claims that their programs are helping people. They are not helping.

Canadians are drowning under 11 years of the government, and occasionally it lifts Canadians' heads above the water for a breath of fresh air and expects them to be happy because the program it is spending too much money on is working. That is the problem.
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate my colleague's service.

I was just sitting in the veterans affairs committee, which is meeting with the Commissionaires. In his speech, the member highlighted that the Commissionaires were never invited to the table, and that can be confirmed from our meeting.

I would like to hear his thoughts about what I asked earlier. The Commissionaires is a non-profit organization that invests in veterans and has confirmed that it has never received any complaints. In fact, it has an 86% approval rating from clientele. I would like to hear what the member's thoughts are with regard to that information.
Mr. Speaker, I thank my colleague for the excellent work he does supporting veterans on the veterans affairs committee.

It was confirmed not only at committee but in court papers that the Commissionaires attempted to contact Veterans Affairs to resolve this issue, but clearly that has not happened. The Liberals are contracting out security services for veterans to American companies. What are the Liberals going to present to Canada next, that they are going to contract out to American companies to provide our military services? This is ridiculous.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Kevin Lamoureux (Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, as we wind up the debate, I want to recognize not only the valuable role but the very existence of our veterans and what they have done in the past. November 11 at 11 o'clock is a very special moment in time when we should all take time to pray and give thanks to our veterans, both past and present. I suggest that all members recognize the true value of that. I would ask them to recognize and appreciate that there are many different things the government does for vets and that all members support veterans in Canada.
We continue to look forward to the fine work that the Canadian Corps of Commissionaires does every day in serving in different capacities, many of whom, 20% plus, are veterans.

Mr. Speaker, indeed, I am sure that all members of this House will say they support veterans, but the members opposite show it in a pretty funny way. If we look at this contract and how they are betraying veterans, or at the other examples that I laid out in my speech, they certainly have a very different way of supporting veterans.

The member mentioned praying. Right now, there are restrictions on the prayers that clergy from all faiths in the military can say. They are not allowed to give religious speeches while in public, which is another way the Liberals are backstabbing veterans.

Mr. Speaker, I would ask for a recorded division.

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, on October 26 of this year, I asked the resources minister if he really respected indigenous rights and, if so, whether he would withdraw Bill C-39. I asked that in response to the BCAFN, UBCIC, Treaty 6, Onion Lake, NAN, COO, APNQL and the Iroquois Confederacy requesting the withdrawal of Bill C-39.

Those organizations represent hundreds of thousands of first nations people. Not only did the minister refuse to respond to me, he had the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Crown-Indigenous Relations respond to me.

I was not quite sure that particular day why the Minister of Energy and Natural Resources refused to respond. I thought perhaps he was starting to agree with me that all the government was doing was building a pipeline to the courts. Then I found out today that more nations are coming forward in opposition to all the new projects that are being designated, nine today alone, nine from the St’át’imc Chiefs Council that consist of and represent, again, hundreds of thousands of first nations, because of the government's failure to exercise its power under the Building Canada Act consistently with the statutory imperatives arising from the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples. They argued that the government rushed the consultation, provided insufficient information about the project and failed to adequately consider its potential impacts on first nations treaty rights.

Cold Lake First Nations is another first nation that has also put forward an application for judicial review. It has also stated it was not properly consulted or engaged at all by the Major Projects Office. It was asking for a designation of the Pacific link as a national interest project to be reversed and for a declaration that Canada has a duty to consult on the project.

Now, I am starting to put things together, and I am hoping to get some clarification today. Whether it is violating the constitutional rights of workers, gutting environmental protections or brushing aside the rights of indigenous people, the government believes that it is above the Constitution and above the rule of law. I am starting to believe that, for the government, perhaps the reason is that when there is a bunch of former CEOs leading the country, they think that they are above our Constitution and human rights.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Anthony Housefather (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Emergency Management and Community Resilience, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, on October 26, first nations leaders met with the Prime Minister and premiers at a historic first ministers' meeting, the first of its kind in 20 years. One of the main topics of discussion was how first nations can develop, own and share in the economic benefits of major projects.

We know we cannot build a stronger Canada without indigenous peoples. That is why we have taken steps to support indigenous ownership and partnership in major projects. We have opened new consultation resource centres to help communities participate in project reviews. We have provided funding so that indigenous communities have the expertise and capacity to engage in discussions about projects that impact them.

We are supporting the growing role of indigenous ownership so that communities can have a stake in what is being built and can share in long-term economic benefits. This includes support using new revenue tools, like the potential creation of a first nations sovereign wealth fund, on which the Prime Minister committed to initiating discussions.

Building on these efforts, the Prime Minister also announced plans to expand the First Nations Finance Authority's lending authority, making it possible for first nations to work together as special purpose vehicles to finance investments in major projects and share in the returns. He also announced $260 million over four years for a new partnerships for indigenous workforce readiness fund. This will help connect indigenous people with jobs created by major projects. These are steps toward greater indigenous ownership, more job opportunities and a direct share in Canada's economic future.

However, creating these opportunities also means getting the federal review process for major projects right. Indigenous peoples must have a meaningful role in decisions about projects that affect their lands and communities and a fair opportunity to benefit from them. That is what the building Canada strong act aims to do. We want to make project reviews more efficient and more predictable while maintaining indigenous rights and environmental protections.

The bill proposes a more coordinated approach, including a Crown consultation hub to bring federal departments together. This would reduce duplication during project assessments and help communities focus their time and expertise on the issues that matter to them. It would also benefit indigenous proponents of economic projects. Under the legislation, when more time would be needed for consultation, timelines could be extended or paused.

I recognize that first nations leaders have raised concerns, but I want to be clear about the government's obligations. Canada's legal duty to consult remains in place. Our commitments under modern treaties and self-government agreements remain in effect, and indigenous rights remain protected.

Building major projects and advancing reconciliation must go hand in hand. Indigenous peoples must have a meaningful role in decisions that affect them and a fair opportunity to share in the benefits. When indigenous peoples are true partners, projects are stronger, communities are stronger and Canada is stronger.

Mr. Speaker, my hon. colleague is absolutely right. We will not be able to build Canada strong without first nations' free, prior and informed consent, something that the overwhelming majority of first nations across the country have indicated the government is failing to do. They are asking the government to withdraw Bill C-39, which violates the Constitution. Just because the government says something, that does not make it true.

It is very clear to workers, environmental organizations and first nations across this country that the government does not respect the Constitution. It is building nothing more than a pipeline to the courts.
Mr. Speaker, I recognize that the hon. member has raised concerns, and I recognize that first nations leaders have raised concerns. We take those concerns seriously.

At the historic meeting between first ministers and first nations, we discussed those concerns, along with how first nations can own major projects and share in the economic benefits they create. The building Canada strong act would help projects move forward while supporting meaningful consultation and protecting indigenous rights.

Let me be clear. Canada's legal duty to consult, our constitutional commitments, our commitments under modern treaties and self-government agreements, and indigenous rights remain protected. Economic development and reconciliation must go hand in hand. When indigenous economies grow stronger, Canada grows stronger too.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to follow up on a question I posed to the Minister of Health regarding the PrescribeIT scandal. I have to say that a week and a half ago when I participated in an adjournment debate on this scandal, I was astounded that the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Natural Resources had the audacity to say that the way the Liberals have handled PrescribeIT is what good governance looks like.

Is it really? We are talking about a failed IT solution to digitize prescription services that cost taxpayers $300 million for a service that almost no one used. Even more concerning is the fact that of that $300 million, 200 million tax dollars are missing and unaccounted for.

There are also the Liberal insider executives who got rich padding their pockets with exorbitant bonuses. Let us take the CEO, Michael Green, for example. He padded his pocket with in excess of $600,000 in bonuses in just three years, between 2023 and 2026. Then he was awarded $1 million on his way out the door after the Minister of Health claimed she had fired him. I can only say that most Canadians would love to have $1 million in compensation upon being fired.

There are at least five other executives who received between $70,000 and $90,000 in bonuses in the same three-year period. We are talking about millions of tax dollars that went out the door by way of bonuses to reward Liberal insider executives who presided over what was a complete and total debacle, if not something much worse.

Then, there is the Minister of Health. Where was the Minister of Health through it all? The minister had completely turned a blind eye. She turned a blind eye as millions of dollars continued to flow to PrescribeIT. Officials testified at the health committee that the minister asked no questions about PrescribeIT. She had no questions about where 300 million taxpayer dollars had gone. The parliamentary secretary says that is what good governance looks like. If that is what good governance looks like, I would hate to see what bad governance looks like.

It is time for the Liberals to stop gaslighting and begin to answer some basic questions such as where the oversight was as 300 million tax dollars went up in smoke as the health minister was asleep at the switch.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Maggie Chi (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Health, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, first, I appreciate a lot of the late show speeches. Monday is a good start to the week. As we go through the session, we have a lot of great legislation going on in the House, including Bill C-39 and a lot of the safe social media bills we are trying to advance also.

As the minister announced in June, our government wants to be sure we are getting accountability and value for money for taxpayers. This why she launched the independent review of Infoway's governance and structure, and a third party audit of the organization's findings. I want to make sure my colleague is aware that the review and the audits are both under way, and we are looking forward to seeing and sharing the results once they are available.

The Auditor General herself felt this was a very strong response, and the last time I checked, my Conservative colleague still respects the work of the Auditor General. She said that any additional work on the file by her would be “duplicative and therefore of limited added value for Parliamentarians and Canadians.” Especially seeing that the member opposite's Conservative colleagues on the health committee were some of the people who asked for the Auditor General's thoughts on the matter, I hope it is a good enough response for my colleague across the way as well.

Mr. Speaker, it is a totally inadequate response. What we just heard from the parliamentary secretary was more gaslighting. Her answer was very much in line with the ridiculous answer provided by the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Natural Resources.

Since she will not answer basic questions, such as where the oversight was, perhaps she will answer a very specific question: Why did Mr. Green receive a $1-million golden parachute on his way out the door, and why did the minister fail to disclose this?

Mr. Speaker, I want to emphasize that there is work under way, and we need to allow the independent auditors to do their work, work that I hope the member will also allow. There is work under way, an internal review of the governance and structure of Infoway. Maybe my colleague did not get the updated QP card from his leader.

Canadians deserve a modernized health care system, and we will always make sure that that is built on the best possible information. Allowing for that third-party review and audit to be completed will do that work, and it will give Canadians the confidence that our money is being spent appropriately.

Mr. Speaker, I am rising to follow up on a question that I posed to the Minister of Natural Resources not that long ago about the Liberal government's failure to remove antidevelopment laws from our oil and gas industry that are hindering our ability to become, in the government's own words, an energy superpower.

We still have, as I pointed out to the minister, a west coast shipping ban. We still have an industrial carbon tax. CEOs have come out and said that Canada is a tough place to invest in this industry because of these issues.
Energy security is fundamentally a geographic issue. Members can think about the news and the Strait of Hormuz, which is a geographic issue.

One place that does not have a geographic issue is the Pacific west coast. Before TMX, exports of Canadian crude to Asia were basically negligible. Today, exports of Canadian crude are reaching Asian markets in significant amounts. In fact, the Asia Pacific Foundation estimates that it is over $500 million per month in exports, which is half a billion dollars of new Canadian exports, because of one pipeline. That is not the only issue.

The barrier is not just getting exports to tidewater. That is only part of the challenge. Canadian crude is a distinctive type of heavy crude. Refineries around the world cannot always switch from one blend of crude oil to another without investments in upgrading equipment, storage, transportation, processing and refining infrastructure.

Canada has another barrier that it has put in front of our oil and gas industry, one barrier that the Liberals are entirely responsible for, because Canada has chosen to restrict one of the tools that could be used to develop these new Asian markets.

When the Prime Minister was the UN envoy for climate action and the financial adviser at the United Nations Climate Change Conference, commonly referred to as COP, or COP26 to be specific, in Glasgow, countries around the world, including Canada, signed what is called the Glasgow statement.

The Glasgow statement, among many other things, forced countries to ban their export promotion agencies from supporting new investments in oil and gas development. Therefore, as an agency of the Government of Canada, Export Development Canada had to adhere to the Glasgow statement.

If we go on their website, they have a policy from 2023, when the government signed on to the Glasgow statement, saying that they are now going to follow this and prohibit investment in those industries. That means that Export Development Canada and other Canadian export promotion agencies can no longer fund or invest in the kind of infrastructure that would facilitate the export of Canadian crude oil, in particular, to Asian markets.

My question to the parliamentary secretary is whether the government will repeal that prohibition so that Canadian export agencies can once again support strategic international infrastructure that expands markets for Canadian industry to, in its own words, make Canada an energy superpower.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Claude Guay (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy and Natural Resources, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, in the words of our finance minister, I have good news for my colleague. There are projects moving forward in this country.

A pipeline is being built from Taylor, British Columbia, to Gordondale in Alberta. There is a major expansion of the sunrise natural gas pipeline system in British Columbia as well. I am also pleased to remind the member that the LNG Canada phase two expansion has achieved a final investment decision and is moving forward. There is significant investment, billions of dollars, going into energy infrastructure in Labrador, and there is a new transmission line being built to connect Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, which will improve the reliability of interprovincial power grids and respond to the growing demand for electricity.

What does that mean? It means workers are on the job site, equipment is on the ground, communities are seeing the benefits and Canada is building again. However, projects do not move forward just by accident. Canada is also changing how our projects move forward. Through the Major Projects Office, we are bringing together federal decision-making, reducing duplication and giving proponents a clearer path from proposal to construction.
The member asked when the next pipeline will be built, and the Prime Minister delivered the clearest possible answer—
Jacob Mantle: I didn't ask about the next pipeline.
Claude Guay: You did last time.

Mr. Speaker, on October 1, the Prime Minister confirmed that the Pacific link pipeline is of national interest. Pacific link is critical to Canada's ambition to become a global energy superpower. Over the next year, the Major Projects Office, supported by the Canada Energy Regulator, will lead the project's federal review process and consultation. By September 2027, the goal is to finalize conditions for this project and advance Pacific link toward construction.

Canadians expect us to build, and they expect us to build responsibly. That means respecting our duty to consult indigenous people and ensuring that consultation helps shape the project, not just reacting to it. It means working with provinces, including British Columbia, because these projects cross jurisdictions and require co-operation to succeed. It means linking new infrastructure to real emissions reduction. In this case, Pacific link advanced with industry commitment to the Pathways project, a major carbon capture and storage project designed to significantly cut emissions while supporting jobs and growth.
Yes, we are moving forward. We are doing it in a way that is durable, economically, environmentally and socially, and that matters.

Mr. Speaker, I am not asking the member about news today. I am asking him about a policy from 2023, which the government refuses to change. I am not asking about LNG or when the next pipeline will be built because it does not matter if someone gets a pipeline built if their customers cannot refine the product. That is the problem with the Glasgow statement. It prohibits Export Development Canada from investing in those types of refinery capabilities around the world, which would increase the market for Canadian oil and gas. This is, as I said in my original question, just one more Liberal policy that the Prime Minister refuses to change, because he was the one at Glasgow pushing these statements. I do not think a tiger can change its spots.

I will repeat my question to the parliamentary secretary. Will the Liberals repeal the Glasgow statement and let Export Development Canada and other export agencies promote Canadian oil and gas development infrastructure around the world?

Mr. Speaker, there is, in a way, common ground here because everyone in the House wants projects built. Everyone wants jobs created. Everyone wants Canada to succeed. There is no point living in the past.

Our job is to move from discussion to delivery, and that is exactly what Canadians are seeing through the Major Projects Office, through new infrastructure, through projects already moving forward across the country, including pipelines. We are seeing projects advance. We are seeing partnerships built early and built to last. That is how we deliver, and that is what Canadians expect.
